title: Create a folder
text:

Creates a new folder within a project to organize test assets hierarchically.

POST /projects/{project_id}/folders
Endpoint URL: https://test-management.testsigma.com/api/v1/projects/{project_id}/folders
HTTP method: POST
Path parameters:
project_id: Unique identifier of the project in which the folder is created.
Request body fields:
name: Name of the folder to be created.
order: Order in which the folder should be displayed.
Response attributes:
message: Status message for the request; may be empty.
data.folder.id: Unique identifier of the created folder.
data.folder.name: Name of the created folder.
data.folder.project_id: Identifier of the project to which the folder belongs.
data.folder.children: Array of child folders, if any.
data.folder.parent_folder_id: Identifier of the parent folder, if applicable.
data.folder.order: Order index of the folder.

title: API Modules for Arcus
text:
API Modules for Arcus

Use API Reference for Arcus to manage all modules like projects, test cases, test runs, test plans, folders, step groups, & settings

Manage modules of test management like projects, folders, test cases, step groups, test runs, test plans & settings using APIs.

---

You can now use API Reference for Arcus to manage all modules of test management like projects, test cases, test runs, test plans, folders, step groups, and custom fields. These APIs support automation workflows and integration with CI/CD pipelines.

Each module includes a set of RESTful endpoints that support standard CRUD operations, status updates, and data retrieval. Authentication is managed via Bearer tokens, which must be included in each request.

excerpt: Overview: API Reference for Test Management Test Management APIs by Testsigma gives RESTful endpoints to automate test operations like creating test cases, managing test runs, and retrieving project metadata Get a comp

title: Overview: API Reference for Test Management
text:
Overview: API Reference for Test Management

AuthenticationTest Management APIs use Bearer Token authentication.

You must include your API token in the Authorization header for every request. This token helps identify the user and enforce permissions accordingly.

Example header:

Authorization: Bearer <TEST_MANAGEMENT_API_TOKEN>

You can generate and manage your API token from here. The token must be kept secure, like a password.

---
excerpt: Overview: API Reference for Test Management AuthenticationTest Management APIs use Bearer Token authentication. You must include your API token in the Authorization header for every request. This token helps identify t

title: Overview: API Reference for Test Management
text:
Overview: API Reference for Test Management

Pagination
When a response includes a large set of resources (e.g., test cases or test runs), pagination is applied to improve performance and usability. By default, the API returns 20 records per page.

Example:

The following request retrieves only 2 projects:

GET /api/v1/projects?name__NEQ=test&page_size=2

In this example, page_size=2 limits the number of results to 2 projects.

title: FAQs
text:
FAQs

1. What is the difference between Ad-Hoc and Sprints?

Both generate test cases using QI Home. The difference is in how generation is triggered and where the context comes from. In Ad-Hoc, you manually attach context sources and click Generate. In Sprints, QI Home detects when a sprint starts in your connected project management tool and offers to generate automatically using the sprint stories and linked artifacts. Everything after generation — reviewing test cases, coverage, test plans, and quality metrics — is the same for both. See the Overview.

title: FAQs
text:
FAQs

2. Why did QI Home skip some scenarios or leave scenario outlines empty?

QI Home generates full test cases for the scenarios it can complete based on your context. For areas where the context was incomplete or where QI Home identified coverage was needed but could not fully expand the scenario, it creates Remaining Scenario Outlines. These are stubs that mark areas needing coverage. Open the Playground and describe the missing scenarios to fill them. See Use Playground.

3. I clicked Not Now on a sprint notification. Can I still generate test cases?

Yes. Go to QI Home > Sprints tab. Find the sprint with To Do status and click Generate Test Cases next to it. See Generate Test Cases.
excerpt: FAQs 3. I clicked Not Now on a sprint notification. Can I still generate test cases? Yes. Go to QI Home > Sprints tab. Find the sprint with To Do status and click Generate Test Cases next to it. See Generate Test Cases

title: FAQs
text:

4. Why is my coverage showing 0%?

Coverage reflects accepted test cases, not generated ones. Generated test cases start in Pending status. You need to review them and click Save to Library to accept them. Once you accept test cases, coverage updates in real time. See Review and Accept Test Cases.

title: FAQs
text:
FAQs

5. What happens to test cases I do not accept?

Unaccepted test cases remain in Pending status and are counted as gaps. They count against your coverage percentage until you either accept or reject them. Rejecting a test case removes it from the gaps count. Leaving it as Pending keeps it as a gap. See Coverage and Gaps.

6. Can I edit a test case QI Home generated?

Yes. Open the test case from the session detail view or from your library. You can edit the title, steps, preconditions, and expected results directly on the test case page.

7. Can I regenerate test cases for a sprint after the initial generation?

Yes. Open the Playground from the session header and write a new prompt describing what you want to add or change. QI Home generates additional test cases and adds them to the existing session. You can also add new context sources before generating. See Use Playground.

8. What is a test library?

Your test library is where accepted test cases are stored. When you click Save to Library, you select a folder and QI Home saves the test case there. Saved test cases are available for automation, test plan inclusion, and re-use across sessions.

text:

9. Why does the Release Gate show "Not Ready" even though I have accepted test cases?

The Release Gate evaluates Release Readiness, which requires test runs to have been executed. Accepting test cases updates Coverage but does not affect Pass Rate, Confidence, or Release Readiness until test runs complete. Execute at least one test plan to activate the remaining metrics. See Quality Intelligence Metrics.

text:

10. What is the difference between Release Readiness and Release Gate?

Release Readiness is a 0 to 100 score that combines Coverage, Pass Rate, and Confidence. Release Gate translates that score into a decision: GO, CONDITIONAL, or NO-GO, based on configurable thresholds. Release Readiness tells you how ready you are. Release Gate tells you whether that readiness meets your project's release standard. See Quality Intelligence Metrics.

11. Do I need the Testsigma Terminal for Agentic Learning?

Only for Local execution. Cloud execution uses Testsigma Lab and requires nothing on your machine. If you choose Local Devices in the Learn and Automate dialog, Testsigma Terminal must be running on your desktop. See Learn Test Case Live (Cloud) and Learn Test Case Live (Local).

12. What happens to the cloud VM when I end a Copilot session?

The cloud VM is released and any unsaved changes are lost. Use Save and End to save your results before the VM closes. If you click Dismiss, the VM stays running and continues to consume resources until you end the session. See Execute Test Case in Cloud.

14. How do I connect Jira, GitHub, or a CLI tool to my project?

Go to Settings > Integrations from the left navigation. Each integration has its own connection flow. Jira, Azure DevOps, Linear, ClickUp, and Confluence are used as context sources for test generation. GitHub, Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Codex are used for Developer Context Mapping. Each has a dedicated setup guide. See Connect GitHub, Connect Claude Code, Connect Cursor, Connect GitHub Copilot, or Connect Codex.

15. What CLI tools does Developer Context Mapping support?

Developer Context Mapping supports Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Codex. All four capture coding activity through an Arcus plugin and push it to QI Home as context using the /arcus:push command. The mapping flow in QI Home is identical for all four. Context appears in Unmapped Context with a tool-specific badge, and you map it to a sprint or Ad-Hoc session the same way. See Map Developer Context.

title: FAQs
text:
FAQs

16. What is the difference between /arcus:map and /arcus:push?

/arcus:map <ticket-key> links the current context to a sprint story before it is sent to QI Home. Running it before you push means the context arrives already mapped and does not land in Unmapped Context. /arcus:push uploads the captured context to QI Home. You can push without mapping — the context lands in Unmapped Context and QA maps it from there. Mapping before pushing is recommended because it reduces manual work for QA and ensures the context is attributed to the correct sprint automatically.

title: Create and manage projects
text:
Create and manage projects

title: What is Arcus?
text:
What is Arcus?

One place for test cases, runs, plans, and reports, with QI Home generating and automating tests.

Arcus is the test management product in Testsigma. It stores test cases and organizes them into runs, plans, and reports. QI Home works inside it. It generates test cases from your requirements and automates those you accept.

What is Arcus?

Core objects

Everything in Arcus lives inside a project. Within a project, you work with a small set of objects.

title: Integrate Azure Pipelines

Before you begin
A project with test runs exists, and you have an API token available to the pipeline as the TESTSIGMA_API_TOKEN variable.
You have an Azure DevOps account.

title: Integrate Azure Pipelines
text:
Integrate Azure Pipelines

Configure the pipeline

Edit the pipeline — In Azure DevOps, open your pipeline and click Edit.
Replace the YAML — Set the contents of azure-pipelines.yml to:

   trigger:
   - master

   pool:
   vmImage: ubuntu-latest

   variables:
   TESTSIGMA_API_TOKEN: $(TESTSIGMA_API_TOKEN)

   steps:
   # Step 1: Build Using Maven and Generate Test Report
   - task: Maven@3
   inputs:
       mavenPomFile: 'pom.xml'
       mavenOptions: '-Xmx3072m'
       javaHomeOption: 'JDKVersion'
       jdkVersionOption: '1.8'
       jdkArchitectureOption: 'x64'
       publishJUnitResults: true
       testResultsFiles: '**/surefire-reports/TEST-*.xml'
       goals: 'package'
   continueOnError: true
   displayName: 'Build and Test with Maven'
excerpt: Integrate Azure Pipelines Configure the pipeline Edit the pipeline — In Azure DevOps, open your pipeline and click Edit. Replace the YAML — Set the contents of azure-pipelines.yml to:    trigger:    - master    pool:

title: Integrate Azure Pipelines
text:
Integrate Azure Pipelines

   # Step 2: Upload JUnit Result to Testsigma Using CURL
   - bash: |
       echo "Uploading JUnit results to Testsigma..."
       curl --location 'https://test-management.testsigma.com/api/v1/projects/{Project_ID}/junit-import/test-run/{Run_ID}' \
       --header "Authorization: Bearer $TESTSIGMA_API_TOKEN" \
       --form "junit_xml=@target/report.xml"
   env:
       TESTSIGMA_API_TOKEN: $(TESTSIGMA_API_TOKEN)
   displayName: 'Upload Test Results to Testsigma'

  Replace {Project_ID} with your project ID from the Arcus
  API, {Run_ID} with the ID from the test run

title: Copilot execution controls
text:
Copilot execution controls

Panel controls

These sit in the panel header throughout the session:

| Control      | What it does                                   |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Pause    | Pauses at the current step until you resume    |
| Back     | Steps back to the previous step                |
| Forward  | Steps forward to the next step                 |
| Settings | Opens session settings                         |
| Rec      | Records the current session state as a step    |
| Restart  | Restarts from the first step, once steps exist |
| Stop     | Ends the execution session                     |
excerpt: Copilot execution controls Panel controls These sit in the panel header throughout the session: | Control      | What it does                                   | | ------------ | --------------------------------------

text:

The panel shows two views, switchable at any time:

| Tab                 | What it shows                                    |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Manual Steps    | The original manual steps, for following along   |
| Automated Steps | The steps Copilot is executing, with live status |

  Switching tabs only changes the view. It never pauses or stops execution.

| Failed          | Did not complete as expected |

text:
Developer context mapping

What gets captured

Two types of developer activity flow in.

Pull requests come from GitHub. With the Arcus GitHub App connected to a repository, every pull request in it flows into QI Home automatically.

Coding context comes from CLI tools. Developers working in Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, or Codex with the Arcus plugin have their activity captured in the background. The developer pushes the context to QI Home when done.

Both land in the Unmapped Context view. Nothing is generated until the context is mapped.

title: Developer context mapping
text:
Developer context mapping

The mapping model

Every entry sits in one of three states.

Unmapped — all context lands here first. QI Home suggests the sprint and story it belongs to. You map it or dismiss it.

Sprint — mapped context feeds test generation for that sprint, and its metrics update accordingly. Context routes to a sprint automatically in two cases: a pull request title or description contains a Jira ticket ID, or a developer ran /arcus:map <ticket-key> before pushing CLI context.

Ad-Hoc — for work not tied to a sprint, such as hotfixes, experiments, or cross-sprint refactors. Ad-Hoc mapping is always manual.

text:
Developer context mapping

What QI Home generates after mapping

Mapping is the trigger. QI Home then produces:
test cases from the pull request diff or captured context, for you to accept, edit, or reject
coverage gaps naming areas of the change with no tests
a test plan organized into Smoke, Feature, Regression, and Deep Regression

Execution results feed the QI metrics.

Developers often raise a PR for work already captured as CLI context. QI Home resolves it:
Context still unmapped when the PR arrives — the two unify into one entry. Prompt history and code changes are analyzed together with the PR diff.
Context already mapped — the PR auto-maps to the same sprint or session. Nothing to do.

A developer who ran /arcus:map early needs no action at PR time; the mapping carries forward.

Coverage and gaps

How the coverage percentage is calculated, where it appears, and how to work through gaps module by module.

Coverage is the percentage of generated test cases you have accepted. Gaps are the cases still pending. Both update in real time as you review, so the Coverage tab is where you decide what to work through next.

title: Coverage and gaps
text:
Coverage and gaps

How coverage is calculated

Coverage = Accepted ÷ (Accepted + Pending) × 100

If QI Home generated 10 cases and you accepted 3, coverage is 30% and the other 7 are gaps. Rejected cases are excluded. Coverage shows at two levels: for the whole session in the header, and per module in the Coverage tab.

After generation

The next steps are the same in both modes.

Review and accept test cases groups the output by scenario. You accept or reject cases individually or in bulk. Accepted cases go into your library.

Coverage and gaps shows the coverage percentage per module. Coverage is accepted cases divided by accepted plus pending; rejected cases are excluded. Pending cases are your gaps.

title: QI Home
text:

Automation

QI Home automates test cases from your library without code.

Agentic Learning (Beta) walks through the steps on your live application. It runs on Testsigma Lab in the cloud or on your local device. QI Home observes each step, learns the interactions, and generates automated steps. A manual test case becomes automated in minutes.

Copilot executes those steps in a browser with a live panel. You can pause, add steps mid-run, and save the results. It also runs any test case interactively, for quick sanity checks.

title: Quality Intelligence metrics
text:
Quality Intelligence metrics

Evaluation order

The metrics read left to right in evaluation order. Coverage asks whether enough was tested. Pass Rate asks whether what was tested works. Confidence asks whether the results can be trusted. Release Readiness combines the three, and Release Gate turns the score into a decision.
excerpt: Quality Intelligence metrics Evaluation order The metrics read left to right in evaluation order. Coverage asks whether enough was tested. Pass Rate asks whether what was tested works. Confidence asks whether the resul

title: Quality Intelligence metrics
text:
Quality Intelligence metrics

Coverage

Coverage measures how much of the generated output you have accepted for testing.

Formula: Accepted ÷ (Accepted + Pending) × 100

Pending includes AI-discovered gaps and cases still in Pending status. Rejected cases are excluded. Coverage appears as soon as cases are generated, starting at 0%. The bands:

| Band             | Threshold | Meaning                                 |
| ---------------- | --------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Good         | ≥ 80%     | Sufficient testing surface approved     |
| Gap Risk     | 60% – 79% | Material untested surface               |
| Critical Gap | < 60%     | Majority of testing surface unaddressed |

The module-level breakdown lives on Coverage and gaps.
excerpt: Quality Intelligence metrics Coverage Coverage measures how much of the generated output you have accepted for testing. Formula: Accepted ÷ (Accepted + Pending) × 100 Pending includes AI-discovered gaps and cases sti

title: Quality Intelligence metrics
text:
Quality Intelligence metrics

Pass Rate

Pass Rate measures how many executed test cases passed.

Formula: Passed Units ÷ Executed Units × 100

A unit is one test case on one machine for automated tests, or one test case for manual tests. Each unit counts once sprint-wide, using its latest result. BLOCKED, FAIL, and SKIPPED count as not passed; NOT RUN and IN PROGRESS are excluded. The metric shows Awaiting execution until one unit has run. The bands:

| Band        | Threshold | Meaning                            |
| ----------- | --------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Healthy | ≥ 90%     | Production-ready quality           |
| At Risk | 75% – 89% | Material failures present          |
| Blocked | < 75%     | Build is fundamentally compromised |
excerpt: Quality Intelligence metrics Pass Rate Pass Rate measures how many executed test cases passed. Formula: Passed Units ÷ Executed Units × 100 A unit is one test case on one machine for automated tests, or one test case

title: Quality Intelligence metrics
text:
Quality Intelligence metrics

Confidence

Confidence measures how much of your committed scope was validated, and how trustworthy the results are.

Formula: Trustworthy Weight ÷ Total Weight × 100

Total Weight sums the priority weights of all units in the topmost _generated_ plan. Trustworthy Weight counts only units that were executed in the topmost _executed_ plan and are not flagged flaky. Priority weights: Critical = 3, High = 2, Medium/Low = 1. It shows Awaiting execution until runs exist.

In practice: if QI Home generated Deep Regression but you ran only Smoke, the unrun units stay in the denominator and score zero. Reject the higher plans and keep Smoke, and the scope shrinks — Confidence can then reach 100%. The bands:

title: Quality Intelligence metrics
text:
Quality Intelligence metrics

| Band       | Threshold | Meaning                                               |
| ---------- | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| High   | ≥ 80%     | Signals are trustworthy; scope mostly fulfilled       |
| Medium | 50% – 79% | Reliability or completeness issues; investigate first |
| Low    | 
  Confidence depends on the nested plan hierarchy — see generated test
  plans for how the topmost generated and executed
  plans interact.

title: Quality Intelligence metrics
text:
Quality Intelligence metrics

Release Readiness

Release Readiness is a 0–100 composite of the three evidence metrics.

Formula: (Pass Rate × 0.40) + (Coverage × 0.25) + (Confidence × 0.35)

Pass Rate weighs most because failures are the most direct broken-build signal. Confidence is second as the trust modifier on Pass Rate. Coverage weighs least because gaps are known unknowns. The score is Awaiting execution until Pass Rate and Confidence both have values. The bands:

| Band          | Threshold | Meaning                                       |
| ------------- | --------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Ready     | ≥ 80%     | All quality dimensions healthy on average     |
| High Risk | 60% – 79% | Release requires explicit risk acknowledgment |
| Not Ready | < 60%     | Fundamental issues; do not ship               |

title: Quality Intelligence metrics
text:
Quality Intelligence metrics

Release Gate

Release Gate is the final verdict: a rules engine over the metrics with three outcomes.

| State              | Meaning                                                     |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| GO             | All thresholds met; safe to release without sign-off        |
| CONDITIONAL GO | Soft thresholds breached; release needs QA Lead sign-off    |
| NO-GO          | Hard thresholds breached; blocked, no sprint-level override |

The worst state across the five checks wins. The checks and their default thresholds:
excerpt: Quality Intelligence metrics Release Gate Release Gate is the final verdict: a rules engine over the metrics with three outcomes. | State              | Meaning                                                     | |

| -------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------ | ----------- |
| Pass Rate              | ≥ 95%        | 90% – 95%          |  1         |
| Critical flaky tests   | 0            | 1                  | > 1         |

The gate shows Pending Evaluation until execution data exists.

  All five checks are configurable per project. A project administrator can
  tighten or loosen any threshold.

title: Work with generated test plans
text:
Work with generated test plans

The four plan types

Each plan draws a different boundary around the session's test cases:

| Plan type           | Scope                                                     |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Smoke           | The smallest set of cases covering critical user paths    |
| Feature         | All of Smoke, plus cases for individual feature behaviors |
| Regression      | All of Feature, plus integration points and edge cases    |
| Deep Regression | All of Regression, plus extended and non-functional cases |

  The topmost generated plan type sets the scope for the Confidence metric.
  The topmost type you actually execute supplies the pass rate. Run only Smoke
  and Confidence reflects that narrow validation — see QI
  metrics.

text:
Database query add-ons

Storing and asserting a value takes two steps. Store first:

SELECT name FROM employees WHERE id = 2

Then reference the variable with $ in the verify step's Expected_Value, such as $Test for a variable named Test.

A script file runs whatever it contains, which is the usual way to set up a fixture:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS employees (
      id INT PRIMARY KEY,
      name VARCHAR(100),
      email VARCHAR(100)
);
INSERT INTO employees (id, name, email)
VALUES (1, 'John Doe', 'john.doe@example.com'),
      (2, 'Jane Smith', 'jane.smith@example.com');
SELECT * FROM employees;

title: Add-ons
text:
Add-ons

Why add-ons exist

End-to-end testing covers a large, varied set of features. Some of them are unique to your application under test. Predicting an action statement for every one is not feasible, so Suite makes the action list extensible instead.

Take scroll indefinitely till the bottom of the page. It suits an application that appends items as you scroll, the way Pinterest does. If your test has to reach the footer to verify a copyright notice, an add-on automates it at scale.

title: Suite REST API
text:
Suite REST API

Base URLs

Testsigma serves each account from a regional host, so the host your requests go to depends on where
your account lives. To find your region, read the host in your browser's address bar while signed
in to Testsigma — that host is the one your API calls use.

| Region | Host |
| --- | --- |
| US | https://app.testsigma.com |
| EU | https://app-eu.testsigma.com |
| India | https://app-in.testsigma.com |

Requests to the wrong regional host fail authentication: an API key is issued by one account, on one
host, and is not valid on the others. If you run Testsigma on-premise, your base URL is your own
deployment's host instead of any of the above.

Three path prefixes then serve the endpoints in this reference. Every endpoint page names the one
that endpoint uses, and carries a region selector that rewrites the samples on that page.

text:
Suite REST API

Authentication

Every request carries an API key in the Authorization header as a bearer token. Generate and revoke
keys under Settings → API Keys.

Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json

File uploads send multipart/form-data instead of a JSON body. Each endpoint page carries a
ready-to-run sample in cURL, JavaScript, and Python.

Suite REST API

Response codes

Endpoints in this reference return one of three success codes. Each endpoint page shows that
endpoint's own example response.

title: Stop a rerun
text:

title: Stop a rerun
text:
Stop a rerun

PUT /execution_results/{run_id}
Endpoint URL: https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/execution_results/{run_id}
HTTP method: PUT
Path parameters:
run_id: ID of the run result to stop.
Request body fields:
canStopAll: Set true to stop all executions, or false to stop only some executions. Defaults to true.
result: Result to set for the execution — e.g. STOPPED.
Response attributes:
id: ID of the Test Plan Result.
execution: Nested Execution object with Test Plan details (id, applicationVersionId, name, description, etc.).
executionId: Test Plan execution ID.
startTime: Epoch timestamp when the execution started.
endTime: Epoch timestamp when the execution ended.
duration: Duration of the execution in milliseconds.
result: Result status of the Test Plan — QUEUED, PASSED, FAILED, ABORTED, or STOPPED.
status: Current status of the Test Plan creation — e.g. STATUS_COMPLETED.
message: Human-readable status message.
executedBy: ID of the executor.
buildNo: Build number specified in the Test Plan trigger call.
environmentId: ID of the selected environment.
totalCount: Total number of tests.
failedCount: Number of failed tests.
passedCount: Number of passed tests.
stoppedCount: Number of stopped tests.
notExecutedCount: Number of tests not executed.
queuedCount: Number of queued tests.
runningCount: Number of running tests.
triggeredType: How the Test Plan was triggered — API or MANUAL.
totalRunningCount: Total number of running tests.
executionDetails: Object with global execution settings (timeouts, recovery action, screenshot option, prerequisite-fail actions, etc.).
totalQueuedCount: Total number of queued tests.
consolidatedResult: Consolidated result across the execution.
consolidatedStatus: Consolidated status across the execution.
resultType: Type of result — e.g. ORIGINAL.
excerpt: Stop a rerun PUT /execution_results/{run_id} Endpoint URL: https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/execution_results/{run_id} HTTP method: PUT Path parameters: run_id: ID of the run result to stop. Request body fields: canStop

title: Trigger a rerun
text:
Trigger a rerun

POST /execution_results
Endpoint URL: https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/execution_results
HTTP method: POST
Request body fields:
executionId: Test Plan execution ID.
executionResultId: Test Plan execution result ID.
isReRun: Whether this request is a rerun. Set to true.
reRunType: Test cases to rerun — ALL_TESTS, ONLY_FAILED_TESTS, ALL_ITERATIONS, ONLY_FAILED_ITERATIONS, or USER_PICKED.
testCaseResultRequests: Array of Test Case result objects to rerun, each identified by id. For data-driven cases also accepts iterationReRunType (ALL/FAILED/PASSED/USER_PICKED) and iterationResultIds.
Response attributes:
id: ID of the Test Plan Result.
execution: Nested Execution object with Test Plan details (id, applicationVersionId, name, description, etc.).
executionId: Test Plan execution ID.
startTime: Epoch timestamp when the rerun started.
endTime: Epoch timestamp when the rerun ended.
duration: Duration of the execution.
result: Result status of the Test Plan — QUEUED, PASSED, FAILED, ABORTED, or STOPPED.
status: Current status of the Test Plan creation — e.g. STATUS_CREATED.
message: Human-readable status message.
executedBy: ID of the executor.
buildNo: Build number specified in the Test Plan trigger call.
environmentId: ID of the selected environment.
totalCount: Total number of tests.
failedCount: Number of failed tests.
passedCount: Number of passed tests.
stoppedCount: Number of stopped tests.
notExecutedCount: Number of tests not executed.
queuedCount: Number of queued tests.
runningCount: Number of running tests.
reRunParentId: ID of the parent execution result this rerun derives from.
triggeredType: How the Test Plan was triggered — API or via the Testsigma app.
totalRunningCount: Total number of running tests.
executionDetails: Object with global execution settings (timeouts, recovery action, screenshot option, prerequisite-fail actions, etc.).
totalQueuedCount: Total number of queued tests.
consolidatedResult: Consolidated result across the execution.
consolidatedStatus: Consolidated status across the execution.
resultType: Type of result — e.g. ORIGINAL.
isReRunEnabled: Whether rerun is enabled for this result.
excerpt: Trigger a rerun POST /execution_results Endpoint URL: https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/execution_results HTTP method: POST Request body fields: executionId: Test Plan execution ID. executionResultId: Test Plan execution

title: AI agents
text:
AI agents

What each Atto agent does, where it runs, what it needs before it can run, and which ones are not released yet.

Atto is a set of agents rather than one assistant. Each owns a single job, and each runs from the part of the product where that job belongs. This page lists all seven, what each needs, and which are still unreleased.

title: AI agents
text:
AI agents

Available agents

Five agents are live. The entry point column is where you actually invoke each one.
excerpt: AI agents Available agents Five agents are live. The entry point column is where you actually invoke each one.

title: AI agents
text:
AI agents

| Agent | What it does | Entry point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Generator | Generates test cases from requirements, files, recordings, and prompts, then automates the manual steps | Atto's Home → Generate with AI |
| Test Data Generator | Builds a test data profile for a data-driven test case | Test Case Settings → Test Data Profile → Generate TDP with AI |
| Runner | Drives Copilot, Run with Copilot, and Agentic Learning (Beta) execution | Copilot in the test case editor |
| Healer | Corrects element locators that fail during execution | Runs automatically when Auto Healing is on |
| Analyzer | Identifies the error type and root cause of a failed step, with the evidence captured during the run | Run Results → Step Details → Analyze with Agent |
| Bug Reporter | Files a bug into your tracker from the Analyzer panel, with the context attached | Analyzer Agent → Report Bug |
excerpt: AI agents | Agent | What it does | Entry point | | --- | --- | --- | | Generator | Generates test cases from requirements, files, recordings, and prompts, then automates the manual steps | Atto's Home → Generate with AI

title: AI agents
text:
AI agents

What each agent needs

An agent that appears to do nothing is usually missing a prerequisite rather than failing.

| Agent | Needs |
| --- | --- |
| Generator | Testsigma Terminal installed, and at least one source attached |
| Test Data Generator | Generative AI features enabled, and a test case open |
| Runner | Testsigma Terminal running locally |
| Healer | Auto Healing turned on in preferences |
| Analyzer | An executed test plan containing at least one failed step |
| Bug Reporter | An Analyzer run on a failed step, and a bug tracker integrated |

| Control | What it does | When to reach for it |

| Resume | Continues from the next step, without restarting | You have inspected the pause and changed what you needed |

Test steps stop updating mid-session, and recording new ones does nothing.

The agent is incompatible with Chrome 139. Delete the whole .testsigma folder and restart Testsigma Terminal. That pulls a fresh agent and restores the session features.

The session will not start because a port is in use.

text:
Learn and execute

How Agentic Learning and Run with Copilot differ, what each takes as input, and which one to reach for.

Atto has two ways to put an agent on your live application, and they are not interchangeable. Agentic Learning (Beta) starts from manual steps and writes the automation. Run with Copilot starts from automation that already exists and verifies it.

title: Learn and execute
text:
Learn and execute

Choosing between them

The input decides which one you want. If you have prose steps a human wrote, you need Agentic Learning (Beta). If you have generated steps that need checking, you need Run with Copilot.

| | Agentic Learning (Beta) | Run with Copilot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input | Manual steps | Automated NLP steps |
| What the agent does | Drives the application, then generates automation from what it observed | Executes the steps and updates locators |
| Your role | Record manual steps when the agent gets stuck | Set debug points, pause, and record |
| Output | A new automated test case | A verified or updated test case |

Both open a Copilot window beside the test case, and both drive Chrome for Testing rather than your everyday browser.

title: Learn and execute
text:
Learn and execute

How Agentic Learning works

You start the agent, and it works through your manual steps against the running application. The chat log records each step with its verdict, and a green tick marks the ones that passed.

The agent is not locked to its own session. You keep full access to the application in the browser throughout, so when the agent stalls you can drive the application yourself and let it pick up from there. Record Manual Steps is the control for that.

When the manual steps are done, you ask Atto to generate the automated test case. It produces NLP steps bound to Testsigma element names, which you then save to the library.

Agentic Learning is Beta as of July 2026. Verify the flow in the product before you build a process around it.

Run with Copilot executes automated steps that Atto generated and repairs them as it goes. Its distinguishing control is Generate Steps in the Copilot panel header, which fills in automation mid-session when a locator is missing or a step fails.

After the run, a banner reports that the steps may have changed and offers a refresh. Take it: the test case in front of you is stale until you do.

Where Copilot fits

Plain Copilot is the third member of this family and the one people confuse with the other two. It executes the steps of a test case you already have, pauses at debug points, and records new steps live while paused. It does not generate a test case from scratch. Copilot Mode documents that session end to end.

All three need Testsigma Terminal running locally. Copilot cannot start without it, and the product says so rather than failing quietly.

Can I run the old Java agent and Testsigma Terminal on the same machine?

Only one agent can be active at a time. Testsigma Terminal detects an existing Java agent and uses it for Copilot and for test execution.

The same one. Testsigma Terminal integrates with the existing agent, and that agent serves remote executions, ad-hoc runs, and Copilot alike.

Not yet. The agent is managed from the Testsigma Terminal desktop application only.

Sources Atto reads

Generation starts from context rather than from a blank prompt. Atto reads any combination of these:
Requirements and tickets — Jira, Confluence, Azure DevOps, XRay, and qTest.
Designs — Figma files.
Files — JPEG, PNG, GIF, PDF, DOCX, XLSX, and MD, up to five at a time.

Build the request

Add the step — Click Create Step and type /api to select the Rest API step type.
Enter the endpoint — Set the URL. It is the base location plus the path, such as https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts.
Pick the method — GET is selected by default. The dropdown also offers POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.
Send it — Click Send. The response appears at the bottom of the screen.

Parameters, headers, body data, and authorization each have their own tab. Fill only the ones your request needs.

title: Quickstart: API
text:
Quickstart: API

Verify the response

A request that returns 200 is not a passing test until you assert on what it returned.

Send the request — The response body appears at the bottom of the screen.
Add the verification — Click Outline, then select Add verification. The field loads into the Verification tab.
Choose a match type — On the Verification → Response Body tab, pick how strictly the response must match.

Five verification types apply to both JSON and XML.

| Type | What it requires |
| --- | --- |
| Strict | Every specified condition matches exactly |
| Strict Order | Every condition matches, and in the specified order |
| Lenient | The essential conditions match; the rest can be relaxed |
| Non-extensible | Only the predefined rules apply, with no additions |
| Schema | The response matches a declared structure, format, and constraints |

title: Quickstart: API
text:
Quickstart: API

FAQs

How do I put dynamic data in a raw POST body?

Reference a test data profile parameter as "@|ParameterName|" and a data generator as "!|FunctionName(arguments)|", directly inside the JSON — "id": "!|Number.digits(int:3)|", "name": "@|DogName|".

My API test case fails. What are the usual causes?

| Failure | Look for |
| --- | --- |
| Connectivity | Can the browser reach anything? Retry, then involve your network administrator |
| Invalid request URL | A path not starting with /, unmatched or empty {} braces, unencoded spaces (%20), or reserved characters (; ? # $ * @ { } =) in the path |
| Authorisation | Wrong or expired credentials on the request |
| Assertion mismatch | The response changed shape — re-check status, headers, and body assertions |

FAQs

Authorisation fails when connecting the org.

Check, in order: the ClientId and Secret (typos, regenerate if unsure), the Environment (production vs sandbox), the Callback URL against the connected app, the app's permissions and scopes, and whether a firewall blocks the authorisation endpoint.

Metadata syncs but the Login NLP fails.

The access and refresh tokens have usually expired, the same connected app is shared by several users at once, or the app's configuration changed in the org. Re-authenticate the connection to mint new tokens, verify the connected app settings, and keep one connection per testing environment.

An MFA challenge appears during sync or execution.

What is Testsigma?

Suite turns plain-English steps into automated tests across nine application types, and Atto generates, repairs, and analyses them.

Testsigma automates tests for web, mobile, desktop, Salesforce, and REST APIs. You write steps in plain English instead of code. Suite runs them on a managed cloud lab or on your own machines, and Atto handles most of the maintenance.

Test case structure

A test case is an ordered list of steps. Each step is an NLP step: a natural-language phrase bound to an element and an action.

Enter robert@gmail.com in the Email Address field

text:
Installation

Install the three local applications that extend Suite onto your own machines, devices, and private networks.

Suite runs in your browser. Three local applications extend it onto hardware and networks it cannot reach on its own. Install Testsigma Terminal to record and debug. Testsigma Agent orchestrates local runs, and Testsigma Tunnel reaches a private application.

title: Testsigma Agent
text:
Testsigma Agent

Install and register the agent that runs tests on your own machines, connect local devices, configure it, and keep it updated.

Testsigma Agent is a small Java utility that runs tests on your own machines and devices. Cloud runs never touch it; anything on the Local Devices test lab goes through it — it queues tests, runs them, and posts results back.
excerpt: Testsigma Agent Install and register the agent that runs tests on your own machines, connect local devices, configure it, and keep it updated. Testsigma Agent is a small Java utility that runs tests on your own machine

title: Testsigma Agent
text:
Testsigma Agent

Why the agent exists

The agent solves two problems.

Running tests inside your network. A corporate firewall keeps Testsigma's cloud away from applications deployed on a private network. The agent sits on a machine inside that network and relays communication between Suite and the local test machine over HTTPS, without opening the network up.

Recording mobile tests locally. The mobile recorder needs details from the app on a physical device — the attributes behind each button and field. Connect the device to the agent's machine and the agent feeds those details to your browser. The cloud recorder needs no setup but adds delay; the local recorder through the agent does not.

It ships with everything it needs: a bundled Java JRE, browser drivers, Appium and the mobile recorder libraries for Android and iOS, and the utilities for local execution and reporting.
excerpt: Testsigma Agent Why the agent exists The agent solves two problems. Running tests inside your network. A corporate firewall keeps Testsigma's cloud away from applications deployed on a private network. The agent sits

title: Testsigma Agent
text:
Testsigma Agent

The agent works in a pull model: it opens outbound connections to the Testsigma server, asks for work, and posts results. Nothing connects inward, so no inbound firewall rule is needed for the agent itself.

Testsigma Terminal contains and manages an agent of its own. Installing Terminal detects an existing Java agent, upgrades it, and takes it over, and only one agent is ever active on a machine. Install the agent by itself when you want local execution without the desktop application, which is the usual case on a CI machine or a shared runner.

title: Testsigma Agent
text:
Testsigma Agent

With an activation key

Register an agent with Activate later, then go to Agents, select it, open Config, and copy the Activation Key. Set it as TS_ACTIVATION_KEY:

version: "3.9"
services:
  testsigma-agent:
    image: testsigmainc/testsigma-agent:latest
    container_name: testsigma-agent
    depends_on: [chrome, firefox, edge]
    volumes:
      - ./data/agent_data:/var/ts/agent
      - ./data/agent_temp:/tmp/agent_temp
      - ./<foldername>:/root/.testsigma/agent/logs
    environment:
      TS_ACTIVATION_KEY: "REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_ACTIVATION_KEY"
      CHROME: "http://chrome:4444"
      FIREFOX: "http://firefox:4444"
      EDGE: "http://edge:4444"

  chrome:
    image: selenium/standalone-chrome:latest
    shm_size: 1gb
    ports: ["4444:4444"]
    volumes: ["./data/agent_temp:/tmp/agent_temp"]

| Argument | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| --TS_AUTO_DETECT_PROXY | Detects and uses a network proxy, including one configured by a PAC file. Suits machines that move between networks |
| --TS_USE_SYSTEM_PROXY | Uses the operating system's configured proxy; combine with auto-detect as a fallback |
| --TS_NON_PROXY_HOSTS | Comma-separated hosts to reach directly, bypassing the proxy |
| --TS_DELEGATE_SSL_VALIDATION | Hands SSL validation to your inspection tool (Zscaler, Blue Coat) instead of Java, clearing PKIX path building failed errors |
| --TS_TRUST_STORE_TYPE | JKS (default), PKCS12, or WINDOWS-ROOT to use the Windows system certificate store |
| --TS_ACTIVATION_KEY | Activates an agent registered with Activate later, using the key from its Config page |
| --TS_AUTO_REGISTRATION_KEY, --TS_AUTO_REGISTRATION_TITLE | Registers and activates automatically on start, using an API key from Settings > API Keys and the given name |
| --TS_AUTO_REGISTRATION_HTTP_PORT, --TS_AUTO_REGISTRATION_HTTPS_PORT | Ports for auto-registration's internal communication |
| --TS_MIN_MEMORY, --TS_MAX_MEMORY | Heap floor and ceiling, in m or g — for example --TS_MIN_MEMORY=1024m --TS_MAX_MEMORY=4g |
| --TS_IS_HEADLESS | Runs browsers without a visible window |
| --TS_IS_MOBILE_DISABLED | Skips mobile device detection, freeing resources on web-only machines |
| --TS_LOGGING_LEVEL | DEBUG, INFO (default), WARN, or ERROR |
| --TS_CHROME_PATH, --TS_EDGE_PATH, --TS_FIREFOX_PATH, --TS_IE_PATH | Explicit browser executable paths, when detection misses an install or you need a specific version |
| --TS_JAVA_HOME | Path to the Java runtime the agent should use instead of the bundled one |
| --TS_AGENT_JAR_PATH | Path to agent.jar when it is kept in a custom directory |
| --TS_ROOT_DIR, --TS_DATA_DIR | Where the agent lives and where it stores its data |
| --TS_ADDITIONAL_JVM_ARGS | Extra JVM properties, quoted — --TS_ADDITIONAL_JVM_ARGS="-Dlogging.file.name=/var/log/ts/agent.log" |
| --TS_ENABLE_GC_LOG | Garbage-collection logging, for diagnosing memory issues |
| --TS_ENABLE_HEAP_DUMP | Writes a heap dump to the working directory if the agent crashes |

FAQs

Do I need an agent for cloud runs?

No. The agent exists only for execution on your own machines and devices. Runs on Testsigma Lab, BrowserStack, or Testsigma Emulator (Beta) never involve it.

Does anything in my network have to accept inbound connections?

No. The agent pulls: it queries the server for work and posts results back. Allow outbound HTTPS to *.testsigma.com on port 443 and nothing more.

Why does the agent run Apache Tomcat?

Tomcat is the local web server inside the agent. It hosts the agent's UI and holds the connection to the Testsigma server that test execution rides on.

The agent will not start — "Port not available".

Only if you registered it as Public. A Private agent is available to the account that registered it.

I already run the old Java agent. Will installing Testsigma Terminal break it?

No. During installation the old agent is detected, upgraded, and converted into the Testsigma Terminal Java agent. Only one agent is ever active, so the two do not compete — and Terminal uses that agent for remote executions and ad-hoc runs too.

My old agent was registered but inactive. Does Testsigma Terminal reuse its name?

Only if it detects the inactive agent. If it does not, it installs a new agent and that agent registers under a new name.

Can I start and stop the agent manually?

You can, but it is not recommended, and stopping it affects Testsigma Terminal. The agent starts automatically when Testsigma Terminal launches. To do it manually, run sh Start.sh or sh Stop.sh from the agent location. Restart on the Copilot home screen is the supported route.

| Authentication server | Validates the key, then assigns a tunnel server for the session |
| Tunnel server | A Testsigma-hosted proxy that forwards requests from test executors to your client |
| Test executor | The cloud browser or REST API client running your test, using the tunnel server as its proxy |
| Remote address | The URL the client resolves: localhost, a private host, or a public site |

Every connection is outbound from your side. Nothing in your network has to accept an inbound connection, and no Testsigma address needs whitelisting.

title: Testsigma Tunnel
text:
Testsigma Tunnel

Reach for a tunnel when the application under test is not publicly resolvable:
An application on localhost or on your own workstation.
A staging environment behind a corporate firewall or a VPN.
A private API endpoint that a REST API step has to call.
An environment your proxy refuses to expose to the internet.

A tunnel is a run-time concern, not a property of the test. The same test case runs against a public URL or a tunnelled one without editing a single step.

A tunnel does not execute tests. Local execution on your own browsers and devices is Testsigma Agent, which solves the opposite problem: the test runs on your machine rather than reaching it. A tunnel also does not persist, and it exists only while the client process runs.

The tunnel name is what a run resolves, so two clients started with the same name collide. Give each environment its own name.

Requirements

The client is a single binary with modest requirements, but it has to sit on a machine that can already reach your application.

The client ships for all three desktop platforms, and for both x64 and ARM.

| Platform | Minimum version |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | XP or later |
| macOS | 10.10 or later |
| Linux | Ubuntu 12.04 or later |

These cover the client process, not the application under test.

| Resource | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| CPU | x64, or ARM 32-bit or 64-bit |
| Memory | 2 GB or more recommended |
| Disk | 100 MB to install, 500 MB recommended |

Two conditions decide whether a tunnel works, and both concern outbound traffic.

services:

    environment:
      - KEY=<API_KEY>
      - TUNNEL_NAME=<NAME_OF_TUNNEL>
      - CONNECTIONS=<NUMBER>
      - INACTIVE_TIMEOUT=<SECONDS>
      - VERBOSE=false

Each environment variable maps to one client option. KEY is your API key, TUNNEL_NAME is the name a run resolves, CONNECTIONS is how many connections to hold open, INACTIVE_TIMEOUT is the idle timeout in seconds, and VERBOSE turns on client logging.

Bring it up — Run docker compose up -d in that directory.

Run docker compose down to stop. The tunnel closes with the container, and any run still using it fails to resolve the URL.

Run the client in your cluster and cloud test machines reach applications deployed in private networks. You build a small Helm chart, point a values file at your API key, and deploy.

Make the chart root and its templates directory:

mkdir -p testsigma-tunnel/templates
cd testsigma-tunnel

templates

Manage a Kubernetes tunnel

A deployed tunnel needs three things over its life: an API key that never lands in a repository, a replica count that matches your test traffic, and a safe upgrade path.
excerpt: Testsigma Tunnel Manage a Kubernetes tunnel A deployed tunnel needs three things over its life: an API key that never lands in a repository, a replica count that matches your test traffic, and a safe upgrade path.

title: Testsigma Tunnel
text:
Testsigma Tunnel

Keep the API key out of the values file

Pass the key at deploy time with --set, and set each key separately when one release holds several tunnels.

helm install my-tunnel . -f my-values.yaml \
  --set 'Deployments.siteA.config.key=eyJhbGciOi...' \
  --set 'Deployments.siteB.config.key=eyJhbGciOi...' \
  -n my-namespace

For a GitOps workflow, store the key in your secrets backend, sync it into a Kubernetes Secret with Sealed Secrets or External Secrets Operator, and reference it from the pipeline. For CI/CD, keep it as a pipeline secret and inject it on deploy.

- name: Deploy tunnel
  run: |
    helm upgrade --install my-tunnel ./testsigma-tunnel \
      -f my-values.yaml \
      --set "Deployments.myTunnel.config.key=${{ secrets.TUNNEL_API_KEY }}" \
      -n my-namespace

To rotate a key, generate a new one in Settings → Tunnels, replace it wherever your method keeps it, and run helm upgrade. The pods restart and pick up the new ConfigMap.

title: Testsigma Tunnel
text:
Testsigma Tunnel

Scale the replicas

Raise replicas in your values file to handle more concurrent test traffic, then run helm upgrade my-tunnel . -f my-values.yaml -n my-namespace. Scale down the same way.

To scale temporarily without touching the file, use kubectl scale:

kubectl scale statefulset tunnel-client-mycompany-production-statefulset \
  --replicas=1 -n my-namespace

A kubectl scale change is temporary. The next helm upgrade resets the count to whatever your values file says.

Scale to --replicas=0 to stop a tunnel while keeping the release and its configuration intact. To make that permanent, set replicas: 0 in your values file and run helm upgrade.

Upgrade the client image

Scale to zero first. This lets the tunnel deregister cleanly before the new version registers.

Do not run helm upgrade while pods are active. The old and new versions both try to register the same tunnel name, and the registration conflict takes the tunnel down.

Scale to zero — Run kubectl scale statefulset <name> --replicas=0 -n my-namespace.
Wait for termination — Watch with kubectl get pods -n my-namespace -l app=<app-label> -w until no pods remain.
Set the new version — Update containers.version in your values file, for example to amd64-1.2.0.
Apply the upgrade — Run helm upgrade my-tunnel . -n my-namespace.
Scale back up — Run kubectl scale statefulset <name> --replicas=<count> -n my-namespace.
Confirm registration — Run kubectl logs -n my-namespace <pod-name> -f and look for the registration message.

title: Testsigma Tunnel
text:
Testsigma Tunnel

Kubernetes reference

Three resources come out of a deployment, and one of them is conditional.

| Resource | Description |
| --- | --- |
| StatefulSet | Runs the client pods under an OrderedReady policy, so pods start one at a time |
| ConfigMap | Mounts the tunnel configuration file, args.yaml, into each container at startup |
| Service | A headless service for StatefulSet DNS resolution. Created only when enabledStatefulSet is true |

The OrderedReady policy is why this is a StatefulSet rather than a Deployment. A Deployment starts every replica at once, and each one races to register the same tunnel name. Under a StatefulSet the first pod registers, and the rest join the session it created.

One key sits outside the per-tunnel blocks: Environment.name is a required string, such as production, and it names every resource the chart creates.

config.headerRules adds HTTP headers to requests for a given hostname, which is how you attach credentials the test itself should not carry. Use X-TS-BASIC-AUTH-HEADER for URL-based Basic Authentication, which works on both HTTP and HTTPS endpoints.

config:
  proxy: 'http://proxy.internal.example.com:8080'
  headerRules:
    - hostname: 'internal-app.example.com'
      headers:
        X-TS-BASIC-AUTH-HEADER: 'Basic dXNlcm5hbWU6cGFzc3dvcmQ='
    - hostname: 'api.example.com'
      headers:
        X-Custom-Auth: 'my-token'
        X-Environment: 'staging'

Each row below pairs a symptom with the cause that produces it most often.

| Symptom | Likely cause | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pod stuck in Pending | No node matches the pool-type selector | Run kubectl get nodes --show-labels and confirm a node carries the label |
| Pod in CrashLoopBackOff | Invalid API key, or malformed configuration | Run kubectl logs <pod-name>, then verify config.key and config.tunnelName |
| Tunnel absent from Suite | Wrong tunnelName, or an expired key | Confirm config.tunnelName, and generate a fresh key if it has expired |
| Connection timeouts during a run | Network policy or proxy misconfiguration | Verify config.proxy, and confirm policies allow outbound connections |
| SSL errors during a run | The application uses a self-signed certificate | Set config.delegateSslValidation: true and run helm upgrade |

title: Testsigma Tunnel
text:
Testsigma Tunnel

Use a tunnel in a test

A running tunnel does nothing until a test resolves its name. For an automated run you pass the name as a desired capability. For a REST API step you set it in the step's own settings.

Open the run panel — On the Test Case Details page, click Run. The Ad-Hoc Run panel opens.
Choose a machine — Select a Test Lab and a Test Machine, then expand Desired Capabilities.
Add the capability — Enter the key, data type, and value from the table below.

One capability carries the tunnel name.

| Key | Data type | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| testsigmaLab.tunnelName | String | Your tunnel name |

The same capability works on a test plan's machine profile, which is how a scheduled or CI-triggered run reaches a private environment.

For a REST API step, open the step, go to Settings, and enter your tunnel name in the Tunnel Name field.

Testsigma Tunnel

FAQs

How do I know whether cloud machines can reach my application?

Open the application URL from a workstation outside your company network, without VPN. If it loads, cloud runs work as-is and you do not need a tunnel. If it does not, the application is private — that is what this page solves.

Why can't cloud test machines access my locally hosted application?

Cloud test labs — Testsigma Lab, BrowserStack, Sauce Labs — run on their providers' networks. A development server behind your firewall, proxy, or VPN is invisible to them, and an app served only on your machine (http://localhost:8080) is invisible to everyone. Run a tunnel, or run on your own hardware through Testsigma Agent.

A run reports the URL as not accessible. What do I check?

Testsigma Tunnel

In order: the URL itself (HTTPS vs HTTP, a stray /), whether it loads in an incognito browser from your workstation, whether the test case carries it correctly, whether the app needs a VPN, and whether the page takes longer than the run's page-load timeout. If the app is under development, personal-machine hosted, on a private company server, or VPN-only, cloud machines cannot reach it without a tunnel.

What does a secured or intranet business app need for cloud runs?

Five things, in practice: whitelist Testsigma's IPs on your server (or run a tunnel), run the agent where local execution is wanted, set the iOS re-signing capability where devices install your app, install the Chrome extension for recording, and add the addons your flows need beyond the built-in NLPs.

Configure the function

Create it — Under AWS Lambda → Functions, click Create Function. Fill in the basics.
Check the handler — Basic Settings names the handler file and the timeout. The handler — hello.handler, say — invokes the script.
Set the inputs — The script carries the plan's trigger details:

#********START USER_INPUTS ********

title: Azure DevOps
text:

Configure the pipeline

Create the pipeline — In your Azure DevOps project, go to Pipelines → New Pipeline and pick your version control system.
Point at the YAML — Choose the repository, then Existing Azure Pipelines YAML file. Starter Pipeline has Azure commit a sample instead. Select the branch and path.
Review and run — The pipeline needs two tasks: run the script, publish the report.

# Azure Pipelines YAML file
trigger: master

pool:
  vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'

steps:
- script: echo Hello, world!
  displayName: Run a one-line script

- task: Bash@3
  displayName: Run Shell Script (./cd-api.sh)
  inputs:
    filePath: ./cd-api.sh

- task: PublishTestResults@2
  displayName: publish test-results
  inputs:
    testResultFormat: JUnit
    testResultsFiles: '**/*junit-report.xml'

title: GitHub Actions
text:

Configure the workflow

Create .github/workflows/ if it does not exist, then add a workflow file per pipeline. The build step invokes the script:

name: Testsigma tests
on: [push]
jobs:
  run-test-plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

        env:

          chmod +x ./run_smoke_tests.sh
          ./run_smoke_tests.sh

GitLab CI

Configure the job

In CI/CD → Jobs, click Create CI/CD Configuration file, or use this job directly:

stages:
 - build
build-code-job:
 stage: build
 script:
 - echo "Calling Shell Script of testsigma"
 - pwd
 - ls -la
 - chmod a+x gitlabcicd.sh
 - ./gitlabcicd.sh

Any bash runner works as-is, Docker included. On a PowerShell runner, adapt the job to the PowerShell variant of the script and use PowerShell 7 or later.

title: Google Cloud Build
text:
Google Cloud Build

Connect a repository to Google Cloud Build and run the Testsigma trigger script from cloudbuild.yaml.

Cloud Build watches a connected repository and runs cloudbuild.yaml on changes. One build step calls the shell script, so a push triggers the test plan and the build waits on the result before anything later runs.

A GitHub repository with the project, a Google Cloud project with billing, and admin on both.
The script (here tstrigger.sh) is committed and executable, keys set.

title: Google Cloud Build
text:
Google Cloud Build

Configure Cloud Build

Pick the project — In the Cloud Console, select or create a project.
Open Cloud Build — Navigation menu → View all products → CI/CD → Cloud Build.
Connect the repository — Under Repositories, click Connect repository and authorise the source.
Add the build config — Commit a cloudbuild.yaml that runs the script:

steps:
  - name: 'ubuntu:20.04'
    args:
      - '-c'
      - |
        apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl bash coreutils
        chmod +x tstrigger.sh
        ./tstrigger.sh
    entrypoint: bash
options:
  logging: CLOUD_LOGGING_ONLY

title: Jenkins
text:
Jenkins

Trigger test plans from Jenkins
Log in to Jenkins and click + New Item.
Enter a name, select Freestyle Project, and click OK.
On the configuration page, scroll to Build Steps and click Add build step.
Select Execute Shell and paste the script below.

TESTSIGMA_API_KEY="<your-api-key>"
TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_ID="<your-test-plan-id>"

curl -X POST "https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/execution_results" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TESTSIGMA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"executionId\": $TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_ID}"

$TESTSIGMA_API_KEY = "<your-api-key>"
$TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_ID = "<your-test-plan-id>"

Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
  -Uri "https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/execution_results" `
  -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $TESTSIGMA_API_KEY" } `
  -ContentType "application/json" `
  -Body "{`"executionId`": $TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_ID}"

title: Jenkins
text:
Jenkins

FAQs

How do I turn the JUnit XML report into HTML?

Get the XML one of three ways: the Testsigma Test Plan plugin writes it into the Jenkins workspace automatically, the Test Results page offers it as a download, or fetch it by API — GET https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/reports/junit/$RUN_ID with your bearer key and Accept: application/xml. Then transform it with an XSLT stylesheet: xsltproc junit-report.xml stylesheet.xslt > report.html on macOS/Linux, or PowerShell's XSL transform on Windows. Any stylesheet targeting the JUnit schema works and controls the layout entirely.

title: Shell script
text:
Shell script

The generic script that triggers a test plan, waits for the result, and saves the JUnit report — for any CI/CD tool.

One script serves every CI/CD tool: it triggers a test plan, polls until the run completes or a timeout passes, downloads the JUnit report, and exits non-zero on failure. Each tool page tells you only where to paste it.

An API key from Settings → API Keys.
The test plan ID, from Test Plans → your plan → CI/CD Integrations, in the REST API call to start Test Plan section.

title: Shell script
text:
Shell script

The API underneath

The script wraps two calls you can also make directly from any REST client.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Trigger | POST https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/execution_results with {"executionId": "<TEST_PLAN_ID>"} — optionally buildNo and environmentId |
| Status | GET https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/execution_results/<RUN_ID> |
| JUnit report | GET https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/reports/junit/<RUN_ID> with Accept: application/xml |

All three authenticate with Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>.

curl -X POST -H "Content-type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>" \
  https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/execution_results \
  -d '{"executionId": "<TEST_PLAN_ID>", "environmentId": "<ENVIRONMENT_ID>"}'

title: Shell script
text:
Shell script

#!/bin/bash
#**********************************************************************
#
# TESTSIGMA_API_KEY -> API key generated under Testsigma App >> Configuration >> API Keys
#
# TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_ID -> Testsigma Testplan ID.
# You can get this from Testsigma App >> Test Plans >> <TEST_PLAN_NAME> >> CI/CD Integration
#
# MAX_WAIT_TIME_FOR_SCRIPT_TO_EXIT -> Maximum time in minutes the script will wait for TEST Plan execution to complete. 
# The sctript will exit if the Maximum time is exceeded. However, the Test Plan will continue to run. 
# You can check test results by logging to Testsigma.
#
# JUNIT_REPORT_FILE_PATH -> File name with directory path to save the report.
# For Example, <DIR_PATH>/report.xml, ./report.xml
# 
# RUNTIME_DATA_INPUT -> Specify runtime parameters/variables to be used in the tests in comma-separated manner
# For example, "url=https://the-internet.herokuapp.com/login,variable1=value1"
#
# BUILD_NO -> Specify Build number if you want to track the builds in Testsigma. It will show up in the Test Results page
# For example, we are using $(date +"%Y%m%d%H%M") to use current data and time as build number.
#
#********START USER_INPUTS*********
TESTSIGMA_API_KEY=eyJhbGciOixxxxxxxxxxxxxxxTNpgv0w
TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_ID=2090
MAX_WAIT_TIME_FOR_SCRIPT_TO_EXIT=1
JUNIT_REPORT_FILE_PATH=./junit-report.xml
RUNTIME_DATA_INPUT="url=https://the-internet.herokuapp.com/login,test=1221"
BUILD_NO=$(date +"%Y%m%d%H%M")
#********END USER_INPUTS***********
 
#********GLOBAL variables**********
POLL_COUNT=30
SLEEP_TIME=$(((MAX_WAIT_TIME_FOR_SCRIPT_TO_EXIT*60)/$POLL_COUNT))
JSON_REPORT_FILE_PATH=./testsigma.json
TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_REST_URL=https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/execution_results
TESTSIGMA_JUNIT_REPORT_URL=https://app.testsigma.com/api/v1/reports/junit
MAX_WAITTIME_EXCEEDED_ERRORMSG="Given Maximum Wait Time of $MAX_WAIT_TIME_FOR_SCRIPT_TO_EXIT minutes exceeded waiting for the Test Run completion. 
Please log-in to Testsigma to check Test Plan run results. You can visit the URL specified in \"app_url\" JSON parameter in the response to go to the Test Plan results page directly. 
For example, \"app_url\":\"https://dev.testsigma.com/#/projects/31/applications/53/version/72/report/executions/197/runs/819/environments\""
#**********************************
 
#Read arguments
for i in "$@"
  do
  case $i in
    -k=*|--apikey=*)
    TESTSIGMA_API_KEY="${i#*=}"
    shift
    ;;
    -i=*|--testplanid=*)
    TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_ID="${i#*=}"
    shift
    ;;
    -t=*|--maxtimeinmins=*)
    MAX_WAIT_TIME_FOR_SCRIPT_TO_EXIT="${i#*=}"
    shift
    ;;
    -r=*|--reportfilepath=*)
    JUNIT_REPORT_FILE_PATH="${i#*=}"
    shift
    ;;
    -d=*|--runtimedata=*)
    RUNTIME_DATA_INPUT="${i#*=}"
    shift
    ;;
    -b=*|--buildno=*)
    BUILD_NO="${i#*=}"
    shift
    ;;
   -h|--help)
    echo "Arguments: "
    echo " [-k | --apikey] = <TESTSIGMA_API_KEY>"
    echo " [-i | --testplanid] = <TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_ID>"
    echo " [-t | --maxtimeinmins] = <MAX_WAIT_TIME_IN_MINS>"
    echo " [-r | --reportfilepath] = <JUNIT_REPORT_FILE_PATH>"
    echo " [-d | --runtimedata] = <OPTIONAL COMMA SEPARATED KEY VALUE PAIRS>"
    echo " [-b | --buildno] = <BUILD_NO_IF_ANY>"
 
    printf "Example:\n bash testsigma_cicd.sh --apikey=YSWfniLEWYK7aLrS-FhYUD1kO0MQu9renQ0p-oyCXMlQ --testplanid=230 --maxtimeinmins=180 --reportfilepath=./junit-report.xml \n\n"
    printf "With Runtimedata parameters:\n bash testsigma_cicd.sh --apikey=YSWfniLEWYK7aLrS-FhYUD1kO0MQu9renQ0p-oyCXMlQ --testplanid=230 --maxtimeinmins=180
    --reportfilepath=./junit-report.xml --runtimedata=\"buildurl=http://test1.url.com,data1=testdata\" --buildno=773\n\n"
 
    shift
    exit 1
    ;;
  esac
done
 
get_status(){
  # Old method
  # RUN_RESPONSE=$(curl -u $TESTSIGMA_USER_NAME:$TESTSIGMA_PASSWORD --silent --write-out "HTTPSTATUS:%{http_code}" -X GET $TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_RUN_URL/$HTTP_BODY/status)
 
  RUN_RESPONSE=$(curl -H "Authorization:Bearer $TESTSIGMA_API_KEY"\
    --silent --write-out "HTTPSTATUS:%{http_code}" \
    -X GET $TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_REST_URL/$RUN_ID)
  
  # extract the body
  RUN_BODY=$(echo $RUN_RESPONSE | sed -e 's/HTTPSTATUS\:.*//g')
  # extract the response status
  RUN_STATUS=$(echo $RUN_RESPONSE | tr -d '\n' | sed -e 's/.*HTTPSTATUS://')
  echo "Test Plan Result Response: $RUN_BODY"
  # extract exec status
  EXECUTION_STATUS=$(echo $RUN_BODY | getJsonValue status)

function checkTestPlanRunStatus(){
  IS_TEST_RUN_COMPLETED=0
  for ((i=0;i<=POLL_COUNT;i++))
  do
    get_status
    echo " Exceution Status:: $EXECUTION_STATUS "
    if [[ $EXECUTION_STATUS =~ "STATUS_IN_PROGRESS" ]]; then
      echo "Poll #$(($i+1)) - Test Execution in progress... Wait for $SLEEP_TIME seconds before next poll.."
      sleep $SLEEP_TIME
    elif [[ $EXECUTION_STATUS =~ "STATUS_CREATED" ]]; then
      echo "Poll #$(($i+1)) - Test Execution/Re-run Created... Wait for $SLEEP_TIME seconds before next poll.."
      sleep $SLEEP_TIME  
    elif [[ $EXECUTION_STATUS =~ "STATUS_COMPLETED" ]]; then
      IS_TEST_RUN_COMPLETED=1
      echo "Poll #$(($i+1)) - Tests Execution completed..."
      TOTALRUNSECONDS=$(($(($i+1))*$SLEEP_TIME))
      echo "Total script run time: $(convertsecs $TOTALRUNSECONDS)"
      break
    else
      echo "Unexpected Execution status. Please check run results for more details."
    fi
  done
}
 
function saveFinalResponseToJSONFile(){
  if [ $IS_TEST_RUN_COMPLETED -eq 0 ]
    then
      echo "$MAX_WAITTIME_EXCEEDED_ERRORMSG"
  fi
  
  echo "$RUN_BODY" >> $JSON_REPORT_FILE_PATH
  echo "Saved response to JSON Reports file - $JSON_REPORT_FILE_PATH"
}
 
function saveFinalResponseToJUnitFile(){
  if [ $IS_TEST_RUN_COMPLETED -eq 0 ]
    then
      echo "$MAX_WAITTIME_EXCEEDED_ERRORMSG"
      exit 1
  fi
 
  echo ""
  echo "Downloading the Junit report..."
 
  curl --progress-bar -H "Authorization:Bearer $TESTSIGMA_API_KEY" \
    -H "Accept: application/xml" \
    -H "content-type:application/json" \
    -X GET $TESTSIGMA_JUNIT_REPORT_URL/$RUN_ID --output $JUNIT_REPORT_FILE_PATH
 
  echo "JUNIT Reports file - $JUNIT_REPORT_FILE_PATH"
}
 
function getJsonValue() {
  json_key=$1
  awk -F"[,:}]" '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++){if($i~/\042'$json_key'\042/){print $(i+1)}}}' | tr -d '"'
}
 
function populateRuntimeData() {
  IFS=',' read -r -a VARIABLES <<< "$RUNTIME_DATA_INPUT"
  RUN_TIME_DATA='"runtimeData":{'
  DATA_VALUES=
  for element in "${VARIABLES[@]}"
  do
    DATA_VALUES=$DATA_VALUES","
    IFS='=' read -r -a VARIABLE_VALUES <<< "$element"
    DATA_VALUES="$DATA_VALUES"'"'"${VARIABLE_VALUES[0]}"'":"'"${VARIABLE_VALUES[1]}"'"'
  done
  DATA_VALUES="${DATA_VALUES:1}"
  RUN_TIME_DATA=$RUN_TIME_DATA$DATA_VALUES"}"
}
 
function populateBuildNo(){
  if [ -z "$BUILD_NO" ]
    then
      echo ""
  else
    BUILD_DATA='"buildNo":'$BUILD_NO
  fi
}
 
function populateJsonPayload(){
  JSON_DATA='{"executionId":'$TESTSIGMA_TEST_PLAN_ID
  populateRuntimeData
  populateBuildNo
  if [ -z "$BUILD_DATA" ];then
      JSON_DATA=$JSON_DATA,$RUN_TIME_DATA"}"
  elif [ -z "$RUN_TIME_DATA" ];then
      JSON_DATA=$JSON_DATA,$BUILD_DATA"}"
  elif [ -z "$BUILD_DATA" ] && [ -z "$RUN_TIME_DATA" ];then
      JSON_DATA=$JSON_DATA"}"
  else
     JSON_DATA=$JSON_DATA,$RUN_TIME_DATA,$BUILD_DATA"}"
  fi
  echo "InputData="$JSON_DATA
}
 
function convertsecs(){
  ((h=${1}/3600))
  ((m=(${1}%3600)/60))
  ((s=${1}%60))
  printf "%02d hours %02d minutes %02d seconds" $h $m $s
}
 
function setExitCode(){
  RESULT=$(echo $RUN_BODY | getJsonValue result)
  APPURL=$(echo $RUN_BODY | getJsonValue result)
  echo $RESULT
  echo $([[ $RESULT =~ "SUCCESS" ]])
  if [[ $RESULT =~ "SUCCESS" ]];then
    EXITCODE=0
  else
    EXITCODE=1
  fi
  echo "exit Code:$EXITCODE"
}

title: Google Chat
text:
Google Chat

Send test plan status notifications to a Google Chat space through an incoming webhook.

title: qTest
text:

Export results with the Post Plan Hook

Assemble the plan — Put the linked test cases in a suite, and the suite in a test plan.
Attach the hook — In Test Plan Settings, select qTest Addon under Post Plan Hook.
Fill the hook fields — API_KEY is a Testsigma API key. PROJECT_ID sits after /p/ in the project URL; RELEASE_ID and CYCLE_ID sit after id= in theirs. OVERRIDE_ON_RERUN set true pushes rerun results into the original cycle; false creates a Rerun #n cycle. TEMPLATE_URL is optional, for customised JUnit output, and must be publicly reachable.
Run — Run Now on the plan. When it completes, qTest Result Link in the top-right corner opens the qTest run.

Leave RELEASE_ID and CYCLE_ID empty and Testsigma generates them in qTest at execution time.

title: Auto-Healing for mobile tests
text:
Auto-Healing for mobile tests

What Auto-Healing corrects

During an Android, iOS, or mobile web run, a locator that no longer matches is replaced with one that does, and the step carries on. A stale shorthand like emai heals into a real locator such as //android.widget.EditText[@resource-id="email"].

Unified projects add Gen AI Auto Heal. When an element recorded on Android fails on iOS, the other platform's screenshot provides the healing context, so the dual-locator pair stays usable on both platforms.

Auto-Healing fixes how an element is found. It does not fix a step whose logic is wrong, and it does not invent an element that no longer exists in the app.

Inspect Android WebViews

WebView elements are only inspectable if the app enables WebView debugging. That is an app-side change rather than a capability: call the static method on the WebView class.

WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true);

The setting applies to every Android WebView in the app.

Screenshots are permitted by default on Android and iOS. A blank screenshot in a result usually means the developer blocked capture on that screen.

On Android, remove this flag from MainActivity.java, or from whichever activity you need to inspect:

getWindow().setFlags(WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE,
        WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE);

On iOS, a third-party tool is usually the thing blocking capture. Remove that restriction so Testsigma can inspect the screen.

title: Debug mobile test failures
text:
Debug mobile test failures

These are the usual causes, roughly in order of how often they turn up:
The app changed, so the element or its locator no longer matches.
The element is unchanged, but the navigation to reach it changed.
The app did not launch, or the build under test is not the uploaded one.
The locator was never unique, and the run picked a different match.
On Unified projects, the step ran on a platform the element was not recorded for.
A real bug in the app under test.

A locator that no longer matches often heals on its own — check the auto-heal badge on the result before touching the element. See Auto Heal.

FAQs

My device does not show up in the recorder.

That is an agent-side problem — cable, USB debugging, agent version. The checklist lives on the agent page.

iOS 16+ hides Developer Mode.

Connect the device to a Mac, open Settings → Privacy & Security, turn on Developer Mode, and restart when prompted.

The WDA process will not start on my iPhone.

Usually the device runs an iOS version newer than the bundled support files. Ask support for the current device support files, then: stop the agent, disconnect the device, replace the <version> folder under TestsigmaAgent/ios/DeviceSupport/ with the new files, start the agent, reconnect.

The iOS app opens and immediately closes.

My runs sit in Queued for a long time.

Every parallel your licence allows is in use, and the queue may be full too. Dashboard → Usage details shows both: Parallel Tests 2/2 means both slots busy, Queue 3/3 means the queue is also at capacity. Wait, stop something, or ask support about more parallels. On local runs, also confirm the agent is reporting — its last request time should be under a minute.

"There are already running sessions for the user."

A previous mobile recorder session is still alive — a forced page refresh leaves one orphaned, or another tab holds one. Orphans close themselves after 2 minutes; to act sooner, go to Usage Details → Mobile Inspector Sessions and stop the old session, then relaunch.

The app force-closes or stops responding on cloud devices.

Suite enables device capabilities by default that security-hardened apps treat as tampering — testsigma.cameraImageInjection, testsigma.networkLogs, testsigma.allowTouchIdEnroll, testsigma.resigningEnabled. Set the offending ones to false (Boolean) in the run's desired capabilities.

Android app data resets between Close App and Launch App.

Android-specific: restarting the app inside one session resets its data, which iOS automation does not do. A desired capability in Test Environment Settings preserves the data. {/ UNVERIFIED: the capability name is only in a screenshot in the legacy page — confirm it (likely an Appium noReset variant) /}

Android apps distrust user-added certificate authorities by default, which blocks proxy capture. The app build must opt in: add a network_security_config.xml under res/xml with <certificates src="system" /> and <certificates src="user" /> as trust anchors, and reference it from the manifest's <application> element.

Can I automate Apple Pay?

Yes, through the built-in Apple Pay addon, on a specific device set only — iPhone XR through iPhone 15 on iOS 15–17. Verify the device against the compatibility list before building the flow.

Entitlement or keychain errors on Testsigma's iOS devices.

Fetch an OTP from a mailbox

This is the reason most teams reach for generators, because a one-time code cannot be stored in advance.

MailBoxFunctions.getEmailOTP takes three inputs: a Regex to match the code, the Mailbox to read, and a Timeout in seconds. A six-digit code is \d{6} with a timeout around 45 seconds.

Related functions cover the rest of an email flow: getLinkFromContent pulls an activation link, urlMatchingRegex pulls a URL matching a pattern, and subjectVerification and contentVerification assert on what arrived.

The timeout is how long the function waits for the email to appear. Too short and the test fails on a slow mail server rather than on a real defect. Too long and every failing run costs you that wait.

All Issues lists every violation. Its search, list, and detail pane match the web report — see Work through All Issues. Compare Runs and Export sit in the top-right corner.
