FAQs

Where do I find an Android app's package and activity name?

The package (com.example.myapp) locates the app; the activity is its "page". With the app open on a connected device, run adb devices, then adb shell dumpsys window | grep -E 'mCurrentFocus' (| find "mCurrentFocus" on Windows). The output shows both — for WhatsApp, com.whatsapp and com.whatsapp.HomeActivity.

Where do I find an iOS app's bundle ID?

Three ways. App Store: take the number from the app's iTunes URL and open https://itunes.apple.com/lookup?id=<number>, then search the output for bundleId. Local IPA: rename to .zip, unzip, and read softwareVersionBundleId in iTunesMetadata.plist. Only on the phone: browse the device with a tool like iExplorer and read the same plist.

Tap and type are slow on React Native or Flutter apps.

Add the appium:waitForIdleTimeout desired capability (String, 1000L) to the run or recording. It stops Appium waiting for the app to report idle between actions.

A tap fails with "Element is either hidden or disabled".

Tap checks three things: the element is enabled, visible, and the locator is right. If it sits below the fold, Suite scrolls internally to find it — but confirm the first two with Appium Inspector (enabled and visible must both be true).

Scroll to Element does nothing in a native app.

That NLP only works when the target is already rendered in the viewport. Swipe first: Swipe from middle to top on the screen (or bottom-to-top for a longer jump, top-to-bottom to go back). If you do not know how many swipes are needed, put the swipe inside a While loop.

Global step timeout

A test plan can set one timeout for every step, and a toggle decides whether it wins against per-step values. The toggle lives under Additional Settings on the run form.

| Test step timeout | Global step timeout | Toggle | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30s (default) | 30s (default) | Off | Global applies, because it matches the default |
| 30s (default) | 60s | Off | Global applies, overriding the default |
| Some steps customised | Updated value | Off | Customised steps keep their own value; the rest take the global |
| Some steps customised | Any value | On | Global applies to every step, overriding customised values |

The pattern is worth stating plainly: with the toggle off the global is a default, and with it on the global is a rule.

text:

Review the differences

Run the test case, then open the result. Each enabled step carries a camera icon: green means the current image matches the baseline, red means it does not.

Click the camera icon to open the Visual Difference overlay. It carries five controls.

| Control | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Highlight Differences | Marks what changed, which is faster than comparing two images by eye |
| Hide Visual Differences | Conceals the markers again |
| Select region to ignore from visual comparison | Excludes an area from the comparison |
| Merge base image and current image | Overlays the two so you can see the shift |

title: Enable mobile visual testing
text:
Enable mobile visual testing

Tune the comparison

A pixel-exact comparison flags things you do not care about — a clock in the status bar is enough. Two settings fix that.

Comparison mode. Strict requires an exact pixel match. Lenient compares against a threshold: at 70%, the step passes when 70% of pixels match. Set it from the camera icon overlay under Visual Testing Mode.

Ignore regions. Draw regions to exclude dynamic content — the status bar, timestamps, user-specific data. Select Select region to ignore from visual comparison, mark the areas, and click Save ignore region.

By default a visual difference is reported but does not fail the test case. Test Case Settings → Fail Test Case if Visual Testing Fails changes that; turn it on only once baselines and ignore regions are settled.

title: On-premise architecture
text:
On-premise architecture

How the containers, database, and agents fit together on your own infrastructure, and which port each one uses.

An on-premise deployment runs Suite inside your own network. Client machines hold the agents, a load balancer fronts a set of service containers, and every container reads and writes one MySQL database. This page lists the pieces and their ports.

title: On-premise architecture
text:
On-premise architecture

The three layers

| Layer | What sits there |
| --- | --- |
| Client systems | The agents that create and execute tests, plus the browsers people use to reach the web interface |
| Central server | The container set that processes and stores everything the agents send, and serves the web interface |
| Database | MySQL, holding test results, user data, and everything else |

Traffic flows one way in. Client systems with the agent installed connect to the load balancer, which distributes requests across the service containers by role. Every container talks to the central database, and each has its own ports for internal communication.

Client systems

Agents are installed per client machine. They drive test browsers and mobile devices, using ports 8383, 8484, 8100, and 5037, plus the range 10000–65535. They send results back to the central server.

The central server is the hub. It processes and stores the data agents send, serves the web interface, and communicates with the database to store and retrieve it. It also provides storage for data and test results.

MySQL is the backbone of storage, holding test results, user data, and the rest. It talks to the central server over TCP on port 3307.

title: Custom domains for on-premise
text:
Custom domains for on-premise

Serve an on-premise deployment from your own domain instead of the default testsigmaprivate.com URLs.

By default an on-premise deployment answers on testsigmaprivate.com subdomains. Pointing it at your own domain takes six URLs and their SSL certificates. Arrange it before Testsigma generates your build, not after.

Tell Testsigma you want custom domains before the on-prem build is generated. The domain names are baked into the images, so retrofitting them means a new build.

The six subdomains below exist in your DNS.
You hold SSL certificates (.crt) for them, either a wildcard or one per subdomain.
The certificates are copied onto the server where the installation will run.

Machine configuration
Install Ubuntu at the root, on a 256 GB machine.
Mount a 2 TB or larger disk for storage, at /data.

Any file system will do — pick what your team knows.
RAID improves disk performance, and is optional.

text:
Install and set up on-premise

Backups

Back up every 24 hours and keep a week of history. Clean old data periodically to protect disk health and free space. Longer retention may need extra hardware, which you can attach to the existing mount point with LVM.

Your IT team owns these backups, taken as disk backups or as backups of the specific data folders.

text:

Network checks

Confirm the server machine has a working internet connection, then open what it needs.

If a firewall is in the way, allow *.docker.com, *.amazon.com, *.amazonaws.com, and *.maven.org. Add *.sendgrid.com to use Testsigma's mail service.

Unblock these ports if they are closed: 3307, 7010, 8080, 8082, 8084, 9090, 9095, 9096, 9097, 4201, 4203, 4211, and 4230. Architecture maps each one to its service.

The application is not accessible

The usual cause is missing host entries. Open /etc/hosts on the server and add <system-ip-address> <domain> pairs for every service:

192.168.0.1 dev.testsigmaprivate.com
192.168.0.1 dev-id.testsigmaprivate.com
192.168.0.1 dev-addon.testsigmaprivate.com
192.168.0.1 dev-visualtesting.testsigmaprivate.com
192.168.0.1 dev-audit.testsigmaprivate.com
192.168.0.1 dev-mobilerecorder.testsigmaprivate.com

Put each entry on its own line. Combining them is a known source of stray binary characters that break resolution.

docker update --restart unless-stopped $(docker ps -q)

Sign in to Docker Hub with docker login -u testsigmaonprem. Ask Testsigma support for the access token.

Almost always folder permissions inside the container, on ts_app_server_data.

title: Install and set up on-premise
text:
Install and set up on-premise

The application is slow

MySQL connection drops and slowdowns are usually connection limits and packet size. Add a command to the MySQL service in the compose file:

testsigma_mysql:
  container_name: testsigma-mysql
  image: testsigmainc/onprem:mysql-<companyName>-<Version>
  platform: linux/x86_64
  restart: always
  volumes:
    - ./data/db_data:/var/lib/mysql
  environment:
    MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: root
  command: --max_connections=1000 --max_allowed_packet=128M --sql_mode="STRICT_TRANS_TABLES,NO_ZERO_IN_DATE,NO_ZERO_DATE,ERROR_FOR_DIVISION_BY_ZERO,NO_ENGINE_SUBSTITUTION"
  ports:
    - '3307:3306'
  networks:
    - testsigma-network

title: Install and set up on-premise
text:
Install and set up on-premise

FAQs

Why does Testsigma need so many ports?

Each port belongs to a distinct micro-service running as its own Docker container, so the count follows the service set. The full mapping is in Architecture. Note that MySQL is 3307 externally and 3306 inside its container.

Which operating system should the server run?

Ubuntu is preferred. RHEL 9.x is the recommended alternative and RHEL 8 is supported — for those, follow Docker's RHEL installation guide.

Can I use my own MySQL rather than the container?

Yes. Map it in the compose file in place of testsigma_mysql, and make sure it meets the database requirements.

The application will not load straight after docker-compose up.

Give it up to three minutes. Nginx needs time to start, and the URL answers once it has.

How much hardware do I actually need?

title: Custom dashboards
text:

Create a dashboard

Switch to Advanced — On the Dashboard, click Advanced next to Legacy. Existing dashboards appear as tabs.
Start a new one — Click Create Dashboard. You can also click Create New + in the top-right corner and select Dashboard.
Name it — Enter a name that says who it is for, such as Release Readiness - Q2 2026. Keep it searchable but short enough for a navigation menu.

title: Auto-Healing for Salesforce tests
text:
Auto-Healing for Salesforce tests

Turn on Auto-Healing, see how it repairs Lightning locators mid-run, and promote a healed locator permanently.

Lightning markup shifts between Salesforce releases, so locators break here more often than anywhere else. Auto-Healing compares the org's current UI against the stored locators during a run and corrects invalid ones. It reports every change, so healing stays visible.

You are an administrator, or someone who can change project preferences.
A Salesforce connection is set up for the project.

text:
Auto-Healing for Salesforce tests

Turn on Auto-Healing

Open preferences — Go to Settings → Preferences.
Enable it — Turn on the toggle on the Auto Healing widget.

Runs from that point on correct locators without anyone intervening.

Auto-Healing works on its own, and the generative AI feature makes it broader: deeper locator analysis and better coverage. If your account has no access to it, Testsigma support can enable it.

title: Auto-Healing for Salesforce tests
text:
Auto-Healing for Salesforce tests

What Auto-Healing corrects

During a run against your org, a locator that no longer matches is replaced with one that does, and the step carries on. A positional Lightning locator like //div[@role='list']//one-app-nav-bar-item-root[5] heals into a resilient one such as //span[text()[normalize-space() = 'Leads List']]/...

Auto-Healing fixes how an element is found. It does not fix a step whose logic is wrong, and it does not invent an element the org no longer renders.

Healing is the runtime repair loop. Salesforce projects also have an explicit one: refreshing metadata after an org change flags every element, step, and test case the change broke, for repair before the next run. See Recover from a metadata refresh.

Narrow down why it failed

Most failures come from a short list of causes. Reading the evidence in order tells you which one you have.

Find the failing step — Open the result. Suite marks the step that failed and stopped execution.
Look at the evidence — Check the screenshot taken at that moment, and the execution recording at that timestamp if one was captured.

title: Debug Salesforce test failures
text:
Debug Salesforce test failures

These are the usual causes, roughly in order of how often they turn up:
A Salesforce release shifted the Lightning markup, so the locator no longer matches.
The org's configuration changed — a removed field, a renamed object — and the metadata is stale.
The user connection could not log in, or its session expired.
The locator was never unique, and the run picked a different match.
A real bug in the org's customisation.

A shifted Lightning locator often heals on its own — check the auto-heal badge on the result before touching the element. For org changes, refresh the metadata: it flags every impacted element, step, and test case. See Recover from a metadata refresh.

Re-run failed test cases

After an org fix or a configuration change, you rarely want the whole plan again. Each test case row carries a re-run icon, and the run header carries a Re-Run button for the whole result.

Clicking Rerun offers three scopes, then Start execution begins it.

| Scope | What it runs |
| --- | --- |

title: Salesforce data generators
text:
Salesforce data generators

Fetch an OTP from a mailbox

This is the reason most teams reach for generators, because a one-time code cannot be stored in advance.

MailBoxFunctions.getEmailOTP takes three inputs: a Regex to match the code, the Mailbox to read, and a Timeout in seconds. A six-digit code is \d{6} with a timeout around 45 seconds.

Related functions cover the rest of an email flow: getLinkFromContent pulls an activation link, urlMatchingRegex pulls a URL matching a pattern, and subjectVerification and contentVerification assert on what arrived.

The timeout is how long the function waits for the email to appear. Too short and the test fails on a slow mail server rather than on a real defect. Too long and every failing run costs you that wait.

The nine test data types a step can read, the sigil that selects each one, and when to reach for it.

Every value a Salesforce test step consumes has a type, and the type decides where the value comes from: typed in, read from a profile, captured mid-run, or generated. This page lists all nine and the prefix character that selects each one.

title: Salesforce test data types
text:
Salesforce test data types

The nine types

Each type has a sigil that identifies it in a step, which is faster than the dropdown once you know them.

| Type | Sigil | Value comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plain Text | none | What you type, fixed for every run |
| Parameter | @ | A column in the linked test data profile |
| Runtime | $ | A value stored earlier in the same run |
| Environment | * | The selected environment's variables |
| Random | ~ | A generated alphanumeric string |
| Data Generator | ! | A generator function, for realistic values |
| Phone Number | — | A Testsigma-provisioned number that can receive SMS |
| Mailbox | — | A Testsigma-provisioned mailbox that can receive email |
| Upload | — | A file in the project's uploads |

title: Salesforce test data types
text:
Salesforce test data types

Plain text

A fixed value, used for anything that does not change between runs: an org URL, a record name, a constant.

To enter a deliberately empty value, use the string key_blank. That submits a blank rather than skipping the field, which is what you need to test a required-field validation.

title: Salesforce test data types
text:
Salesforce test data types

Parameter

Reads a named column from the test data profile linked to the test case. Write @Email for a column called Email.

A parameter only resolves if the test case is linked to the profile that holds it. Link the profile first, then the step repeats once per data set. An unlinked parameter fails at run time, not at authoring time.
excerpt: Salesforce test data types Parameter Reads a named column from the test data profile linked to the test case. Write @Email for a column called Email. A parameter only resolves if the test case is linked to the profile

title: Salesforce test data types
text:
Salesforce test data types

Runtime

Holds a value captured during the run. A step using the Store keyword writes it, and later steps read it with $.

Read the report

Once the plan finishes, click View Reports for that plan, then View Report at the bottom to open the detailed accessibility report. It has two tabs.

Overview summarises the run. Issue Overview is a donut chart grouping findings as Critical, Serious, Moderate, Minor, or Success. Issues by WCAG Principle organises them under Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust, with the failed criteria under each. Issues by Pages lists every URL scanned and how many checks failed on it. Issues by Components groups by HTML element type, which is how a custom component failing on every page shows itself.

The Best Practices tab carries the remediation guidance. The report tells you what failed; that tab tells you what to do about it. For standard Lightning components the fix usually belongs in your customisation, not the component.

title: Step options and settings
text:
Step options and settings

Global step timeout

A test plan can set one timeout for every step, and a toggle decides whether it wins against per-step values. The toggle lives under Additional Settings on the run form.

| Test step timeout | Global step timeout | Toggle | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30s (default) | 30s (default) | Off | Global applies, because it matches the default |
| 30s (default) | 60s | Off | Global applies, overriding the default |
| Some steps customised | Updated value | Off | Customised steps keep their own value; the rest take the global |
| Some steps customised | Any value | On | Global applies to every step, overriding customised values |

The pattern is worth stating plainly: with the toggle off the global is a default, and with it on the global is a rule.

title: Salesforce step types
text:
Salesforce step types

Standard step types

These seven cover the body of most test cases.

| Step type | Command | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Natural Language | / | A single action or assertion written in Testsigma's readable syntax |
| Step Group | /stepgroup | A reusable sequence of steps, maintained in one place |
| Create a Block | /blocks | A labelled group of steps inside one test case, for structure rather than reuse |
| For Loop | /forloop | Repeat a set of steps a fixed number of times, or once per data row |
| While Loop | /whileloop | Repeat a set of steps until a condition stops being true |

title: Salesforce step types
text:
Salesforce step types

Conditional step types

Each of these wraps a standard type in a condition, so the wrapped step runs only when the condition holds.

| Step type | Command | What it wraps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| If Natural Language | /if | A natural-language step |
| If Step Group | /if stepgroup | A step group |
| If Custom Function | /if function | A custom function |
| If Rest API | /if api | A REST API step |

REST API steps work in any test case, not only Rest API projects. Setting state through the API and verifying it in the org beats driving both through the UI.

text:

Review the differences

Run the test case, then open the result. Each enabled step carries a camera icon: green means the current image matches the baseline, red means it does not.

Click the camera icon to open the Visual Difference overlay. It carries five controls.

| Control | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Highlight Differences | Marks what changed, which is faster than comparing two images by eye |
| Hide Visual Differences | Conceals the markers again |

title: Enable Salesforce visual testing
text:
Enable Salesforce visual testing

Tune the comparison

A pixel-exact comparison flags things you do not care about. Record pages are full of dynamic content — record names, timestamps, list counts — and every one is a false positive waiting to happen.

Comparison mode. Strict requires an exact pixel match. Lenient compares against a threshold: at 70%, the step passes when 70% of pixels match. Set it from the camera icon overlay under Visual Testing Mode.

Ignore regions. Draw regions to exclude the dynamic areas. Select Select region to ignore from visual comparison, mark them, and click Save ignore region.

By default a visual difference is reported but does not fail the test case. Test Case Settings → Fail Test Case if Visual Testing Fails changes that; turn it on only once baselines and ignore regions are settled.

title: Import test cases between projects
text:
Import test cases between projects

The review list marks what the import will do to each test case:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| New | Does not exist in the destination — it is created |
| No Change | Exists and is identical — nothing happens |
| Override | Exists but differs — the import replaces it |

"Invalid certificate uploaded."

The certificate is corrupt or was not generated from the CSR that Testsigma produced for this profile.

Control who can stop executions

Turning this on stops one person ending a run someone else is depending on. It is off by default.

If the toggle is not there, the feature is not enabled for your account. Email support@testsigma.com or use the in-app Chat and ask for it.

title: Team management
text:
Team management

The six roles

| Role | What it can do |
| --- | --- |
| Account Administrator | Everything a Super Administrator can, plus billing information for the account |
| Super Administrator | Complete control over the project, but no access to account or billing information |
| Test Manager | Manages multiple projects, including assigning users and adding applications and versions in each |
| Test Lead | Manages everything in the assigned project, including its applications and versions |

| Read Only | Views the project's contents and changes nothing |

Account Administrator and Super Administrator differ on one thing only: billing. If someone needs full control but should not see billing, Super Administrator is the role.

Auto-Healing for web tests

Turn on Auto-Healing, understand what it corrects during a run, and promote a healed locator permanently.

Broken locators are the usual reason a healthy suite decays. Auto-Healing detects that your application changed, compares the current UI against the stored locators, and corrects invalid ones during the run. It reports every change, so healing is visible rather than silent.

Enable it — Turn on the toggle on the Auto Healing widget.

title: Auto-Healing for web tests
text:
Auto-Healing for web tests

What Auto-Healing corrects

It applies to more than one surface of a web project, and the mechanism differs slightly on each.

| Where | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Web tests | Compares the current UI to stored locators and replaces the invalid ones mid-run |
| AI-generated test cases | Replaces the dummy locators Atto writes when it automates a case without learning the live application |
| Copilot sessions | Validates locators while you debug in a live session, rather than only during a plan run |

Auto-Healing fixes how an element is found. It does not fix a step whose logic is wrong, and it does not invent an element that no longer exists.

title: Auto-Healing for web tests
text:
Auto-Healing for web tests

What a heal looks like

The pattern is always the same: a locator that no longer matches is replaced with one that does, and the step carries on.

| Case | Locator before | Locator after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Web | input["email"] | input[id="email"] |
| Atto-generated | A dummy locator | //input[@id='email'] |

Dummy locators are specific to Atto. If you generate a test case and automate it without learning the live application, the elements carry placeholders — Gen AI Auto-Healing is the part that resolves those into real locators at run time.

By country

geoLocation takes a two-letter country code, such as AR for Argentina. It works for web and mobile web.

These 48 countries are available: Argentina (AR), Australia (AU), Austria (AT), Belgium (BE), Brazil (BR), Bulgaria (BG), Canada (CA), Chile (CL), China (CN), Croatia (HR), Czech Republic (CZ), Denmark (DK), Egypt (EG), Finland (FI), France (FR), Germany (DE), Greece (GR), Hong Kong (HK), Hungary (HU), Iceland (IS), India (IN), Indonesia (ID), Ireland (IE), Israel (IL), Italy (IT), Japan (JP), Jordan (JO), Malaysia (MY), Mexico (MX), Netherlands (NL), New Zealand (NZ), Norway (NO), Philippines (PH), Poland (PL), Portugal (PT), Russia (RU), Singapore (SG), South Africa (ZA), South Korea (KR), Spain (ES), Sweden (SE), Switzerland (CH), Taiwan (TW), Thailand (TH), Turkey (TR), Ukraine (UA), United Kingdom (GB), United States (US).

title: Desired capabilities for web runs
text:
Desired capabilities for web runs

By coordinates

Chrome needs the permission row and the coordinate row together. The three coordinate values are latitude, longitude, and altitude, so 51.50735, -0.12776, 100 is Trafalgar Square in London, and 40.783840, -73.965550, 33 is Central Park in New York.

Firefox takes it all in the profile instead, where the values are latitude, longitude, and accuracy. The example above resolves to Downtown Los Angeles; Central Park would be {"location": {"lat": 40.783840, "lng": -73.965550}, "accuracy": 100.0}.

Geolocation is not supported in Internet Explorer or Safari. Use mapcoordinates.net to find coordinates, and mycurrentlocation.net inside the run to confirm what the browser reports.

Basic authentication in Safari

Safari blocks credentials passed in the URL, which breaks the usual automated basic-auth login. An encoded Authorization header gets around it.

Generate the header — Use a basic auth header generator with your username and password.
Open the run panel — On Test Case Details, click Run.
Pick a macOS machine — Select the macOS version, Browser, and Resolution.
Add the capability — Enter testsigma.customHeaders as the Key, select String, and set the value to { "Authorization": "Basic <token>" }.
Run it — Click Run Now, then check the step-level screenshot to confirm the login worked.

testsigma.customHeaders is Safari-only. On other browsers, credentials in the URL still work.

title: Debug web test failures
text:

These are the usual causes, roughly in order of how often they turn up:
The application changed, so the element or its locator no longer matches.
The element is unchanged, but the navigation to reach it changed.
The application or the API did not load.
The locator was never unique, and the run picked a different match.
Add-on code did not behave as expected.
A real bug in the application under test.

A test that fails intermittently is usually a locator matching several elements rather than a flaky application. See Elements for counting matches in DevTools.

title: Web elements
text:
Web elements

Supported locator types

Seven locator mechanisms are available. Which one you pick decides how brittle the element is.

| Locator | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| XPath | The most flexible. Most other locators can be expressed as one |
| CSS Selector | Matches on tag, id, class, and attributes. The only locator that reaches inside Shadow DOM |
| Link Text and Partial Link Text | Simple, but only safe when the text is unique on the page |
| ID | Stable when the application sets it deliberately |
| Name | Common on form fields |
| Class Name | Often shared across many elements |
| Tag Name | Broadest, and rarely unique on its own |

With duplicate link text, such as the same link in a header and a footer, the action lands on the first match. That is a test that passes for the wrong reason.

Locate an element inside Shadow DOM

Shadow DOM hides markup from the main document, so a shadow element does not exist in the DOM the recorder normally searches.

To check whether a page uses it, right-click and select Inspect, expand the <body> tag, and look for #shadow-root. If it is there, use a CSS selector: it is the only supported locator that crosses the shadow boundary.

text:

FAQs

The recorder shows a blank screen.

Chrome's cookie settings are blocking it. In Settings → Privacy and security → Third-party cookies, enable Block third-party cookies in Incognito mode (not the blanket block), then record again.

A step fails because the captured link text differs from what I see.

The UI may render text in a different case than the HTML carries it (SUBMIT on screen, Submit in the source). The recorder captures from the HTML. Compare the captured text against the page source and correct the element to match the HTML.

I cannot capture or select from a dropdown.

It depends on how the dropdown is built. A real <select> tag works with the Select option... NLPs — by value, text, or index, single or multiple. A dropdown built from div, a, or span is not a select at all: capture the elements it is made of and drive it with Click steps.

title: Web elements
text:
Web elements

Check/uncheck fails on something that looks like a checkbox.

The check/uncheck NLPs verify the element's type attribute is checkbox, and fail when a different tag is doing the visual work. Find the tag actually receiving the click, capture an element for it, and use the Click NLP instead. The same applies to radio buttons and the select/unselect NLPs: no type="radio", no select — click it.

Element not found — what are the usual causes?

Three: the element is not on the current page (an earlier step passed but did not do what you expected — check its screenshot), the locator has a typo, or the element sits inside a frame — switch first with Switch to the frame UI identifier (or by index or name).

The step passes but acts on the wrong element.

title: Web elements
text:
Web elements

Your locator matches more than one element, and the first match wins. //input[@type='password'] on a page with two password fields always hits the first. Make the XPath unique.

The element is hidden, disabled, or not there yet.

Dynamically created elements may not exist at the moment the step runs. Add a wait step for the element before acting on it.

How do applications disable, hide, and check elements?

Knowing the mechanism tells you what a step can and cannot do. Disabled: the disabled attribute (button, input, select, textarea...) makes an element unclickable, and readonly (input, textarea) allows focus and copy but not modification. Hidden: display: none, the hidden attribute, or zero width and height. Checked/selected: the checked attribute on checkboxes and radios, selected on options — which is what the check/select NLPs verify before acting.

My tests sit in Queued for a long time.

Usually every parallel your licence allows is already in use. Click Usage details on the Dashboard: Parallel Tests 2/2 means both slots are busy, and queued runs wait until one frees. Pages load slowly only in cloud executions.

Rendering differences on cloud machines can stall a page. Add the step Click on the Refresh button in the browser immediately before the step that fails on load time.

title: Data generators
text:
Data generators

Fetch an OTP from a mailbox

This is the reason most teams reach for generators, because a one-time code cannot be stored in advance.

MailBoxFunctions.getEmailOTP takes three inputs: a Regex to match the code, the Mailbox to read, and a Timeout in seconds. A six-digit code is \d{6} with a timeout around 45 seconds.

Related functions cover the rest of an email flow: getLinkFromContent pulls an activation link, urlMatchingRegex pulls a URL matching a pattern, and subjectVerification and contentVerification assert on what arrived.

The timeout is how long the function waits for the email to appear. Too short and the test fails on a slow mail server rather than on a real defect. Too long and every failing run costs you that wait.

Holds a value captured during the run. A step using the Store keyword writes it, and later steps read it with $.

FAQs

Why does recording need a Chrome extension?

Modern UI frameworks build pages from generic div and span tags, so a test needs locators into the DOM to act on anything. The extension captures those locators as elements and turns your actions into steps. It does not track browsing outside the application, collect passwords or IP addresses, or modify your application's source; client-server traffic runs over a secure connection.

The extension says third-party cookies are blocked.

Open chrome://settings/cookies and select Allow all cookies or Block third-party cookies in Incognito.

The extension cannot access local files and URLs.

In Chrome, go to Manage Extensions → Testsigma Extension → Details and turn on Allow access to File URLs.

Can I automate a CAPTCHA?
excerpt: Author web tests FAQs Why does recording need a Chrome extension? Modern UI frameworks build pages from generic div and span tags, so a test needs locators into the DOM to act on anything. The extension captures those

title: Author web tests
text:
Author web tests

Technically sometimes, practically no — CAPTCHA exists to defeat automation and keeps evolving. The industry practice is to bypass it in the test environment so tests never meet it.

How do I get past basic authentication?

Put the credentials in the URL of the navigate step: https://username:password@hostname. Use HTTPS, or the credentials travel in the clear. On Safari and mobile web this form slows each step; pass a header instead with the testsigma.customHeaders capability — {"Authorization":"Basic <base64 of username:password>"}.

title: Author web tests
text:
Author web tests

An isolated, sandboxed build of Chrome used only for automation — it never touches your user data, cookies, or history. It downloads automatically once an agent registers and appears in the browser list for executions; Copilot sessions use it by default. New accounts have it out of the box; existing accounts can ask support to enable it.

The site shows a text CAPTCHA I cannot bypass. Can a test read it?

Yes, with the OCR_ExtractText addon from Addons. Capture two elements — the CAPTCHA image and its input field — then in the test: extract text from the image element into a runtime variable with the addon's NLP, and type that variable into the input. Prefer bypassing CAPTCHA in the test environment when you can.

Install the Google Authenticator browser extension, screenshot the QR code your app shows, and upload it under Test Data → Uploads. The extension reads the QR from the upload and generates the time-based code, which your test reads and types like any other value. Username/password, 2FA via mailbox or phone number, and API-key authentication are the other supported routes.

Can I test a Chrome extension itself?

Yes. Get the extension's CRX file (a CRX viewer downloads it; note the extension's unique ID and its popup.html). Locally, put the CRX in the agent folder and pass its path in the Extensions desired capability; in Testsigma Lab, upload it and reference the upload. Then drive popup.html like any page.

text:

Global step timeout

A test plan can set one timeout for every step, and a toggle decides whether it wins against per-step values. The toggle lives under Additional Settings on the run form.

| Test step timeout | Global step timeout | Toggle | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30s (default) | 30s (default) | Off | Global applies, because it matches the default |
| 30s (default) | 60s | Off | Global applies, overriding the default |
| Some steps customised | Updated value | Off | Customised steps keep their own value; the rest take the global |
| Some steps customised | Any value | On | Global applies to every step, overriding customised values |

The pattern is worth stating plainly: with the toggle off the global is a default, and with it on the global is a rule.

FAQs

How do I drag and drop?

Use Drag the element and drop on the element element: the first element is what you drag, the second is where it lands.

How do I upload a file?

Upload file test data using the element, where the test data is a Testsigma Cloud Storage path (testsigma-storage:/...), a public URL (S3, Google Drive, Dropbox), or a local path. Local paths work only on your own machines through the agent — cloud labs cannot see your file system.

How do I click something that is not always there?

Click on element if visible passes when the element is visible and skips without failing when it exists but is hidden. It still fails if the element is missing from the DOM entirely; wrap the click in an If conditional step to survive that too.

A text field returns nothing when I store its text.

title: Step types
text:
Step types

<input> and <textarea> keep their content in the value attribute, not as inner text. Use Store the value for the attribute attribute of the element element into a variable test data with value, instead of the Store text... step. Inspect the element: text between tags wants Store text, text in an attribute wants Store the value.

Why clear cookies or close tabs at the start of a test?

Long runs exhaust the test machine's disk and crash the browser, especially against apps that leak memory or open many tabs. Start tests with Delete all cookies from the current session and close spare windows with Close all windows except the current window (or the other close-window variants).

How do I press keys that are not text?

Press Test Data key, with the key's value as the test data.

Narrow down why it failed

Most failures come from a short list of causes. Reading the evidence in order tells you which one you have.

Find the failing step — Open the result. Suite marks the step that failed and stopped execution.
Look at the evidence — Check the screenshot taken at that moment against what the step expected.

title: Debug desktop test failures
text:
Debug desktop test failures

These are the usual causes, roughly in order of how often they turn up:
The application changed, so a learned object no longer matches. Re-learn it — see Elements.
The application was not open on the machine, or a different version was.
The machine was locked, or its screen state differed from when the objects were learned.
The agent on the machine was offline, so the run never started.
A real bug in the application under test.

Desktop (Beta) runs execute only on your own Windows machines, so the machine's state — logged-in session, open application, application version — is part of every failure investigation.

Re-run failed test cases

After an application fix, you rarely want the whole plan again. Each test case row carries a re-run icon, and the run header carries a Re-Run button for the whole result.

Clicking Rerun offers three scopes, then Start execution begins it.

title: Desktop data generators
text:
Desktop data generators

Fetch an OTP from a mailbox

This is the reason most teams reach for generators, because a one-time code cannot be stored in advance.

MailBoxFunctions.getEmailOTP takes three inputs: a Regex to match the code, the Mailbox to read, and a Timeout in seconds. A six-digit code is \d{6} with a timeout around 45 seconds.

Related functions cover the rest of an email flow: getLinkFromContent pulls an activation link, urlMatchingRegex pulls a URL matching a pattern, and subjectVerification and contentVerification assert on what arrived.

The timeout is how long the function waits for the email to appear. Too short and the test fails on a slow mail server rather than on a real defect. Too long and every failing run costs you that wait.

text:

Global step timeout

A test plan can set one timeout for every step, and a toggle decides whether it wins against per-step values. The toggle lives under Additional Settings on the run form.

| Test step timeout | Global step timeout | Toggle | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30s (default) | 30s (default) | Off | Global applies, because it matches the default |
| 30s (default) | 60s | Off | Global applies, overriding the default |
| Some steps customised | Updated value | Off | Customised steps keep their own value; the rest take the global |
| Some steps customised | Any value | On | Global applies to every step, overriding customised values |

The pattern is worth stating plainly: with the toggle off the global is a default, and with it on the global is a rule.

Most failures come from a short list of causes. Reading the evidence in order tells you which one you have.

title: Debug Windows (Lite) test failures
text:
Debug Windows (Lite) test failures

These are the usual causes, roughly in order of how often they turn up:
The application changed, so a captured element no longer matches. Recapture it with the Recorder — see Elements.
The application did not open on the machine, or opened a different version.
The machine was locked, or its screen state differed from when the elements were captured.
The Agent on the machine was offline, so the run never started.
A real bug in the application under test.

Windows (Lite) runs execute only on your own machines through the Testsigma Agent, so the machine's state — logged-in session, screen resolution, application version — is part of every failure investigation.

Pull the logs — Collect the Agent logs from the machine. Set the log level and send logs covers raising the level to DEBUG and sharing them with support.

text:
Windows (Lite) run results

Re-run failed test cases

After an application fix, you rarely want the whole plan again. Each test case row carries a re-run icon, and the run header carries a Re-Run button for the whole result.

Clicking Rerun offers three scopes, then Start execution begins it.

| Scope | What it runs |
| --- | --- |
| All Test Cases | Every case in the selected run |
| All Failed Test Cases | Only the cases that failed |
| Select Cases for Re-Run | The cases you tick |

A re-run executes your current test cases, not the versions that produced the original result. If someone edited a case since, you are testing something else. The target machine must also be online — a re-run needs its Agent, the same as the original run.

Each run ID allows at most 10 reruns. Reruns accumulate against the original run rather than starting a fresh history, so spend them deliberately.

title: Windows (Lite) data generators
text:
Windows (Lite) data generators

Fetch an OTP from a mailbox

This is the reason most teams reach for generators, because a one-time code cannot be stored in advance.

MailBoxFunctions.getEmailOTP takes three inputs: a Regex to match the code, the Mailbox to read, and a Timeout in seconds. A six-digit code is \d{6} with a timeout around 45 seconds.

Related functions cover the rest of an email flow: getLinkFromContent pulls an activation link, urlMatchingRegex pulls a URL matching a pattern, and subjectVerification and contentVerification assert on what arrived.

The timeout is how long the function waits for the email to appear. Too short and the test fails on a slow mail server rather than on a real defect. Too long and every failing run costs you that wait.

The nine types

| Plain Text | none | What you type, fixed for every run |
| Parameter | @ | A column in the linked test data profile |

text:
Windows (Lite) test data types

Plain text

A fixed value, used for anything that does not change between runs: a file path, a label, a constant.

To enter a deliberately empty value, use the string key_blank. That submits a blank rather than skipping the field, which is what you need to test a required-field validation.

text:
Windows (Lite) test data types

Parameter

Reads a named column from the test data profile linked to the test case. Write @Email for a column called Email.

A parameter only resolves if the test case is linked to the profile that holds it. Link the profile first, then the step repeats once per data set. An unlinked parameter fails at run time, not at authoring time.

title: Windows (Lite) test data types
text:
Windows (Lite) test data types

Runtime

Holds a value captured during the run. A step using the Store keyword writes it, and later steps read it with $.

This is how you assert on something the application generated: store a value one screen produces, then verify it where it appears next. Runtime values live for the run, not beyond it.

title: Windows (Lite) test data types
text:
Windows (Lite) test data types

Environment

Reads from the environment selected for the run, so one test case works against development, staging, UAT, and production without edits. Write * followed by the variable name.

Server names, file paths, and connection details belong here. Environment variables are scoped to the project.

Renaming an environment variable changes it across every environment in the project, not just the one you are editing. The product warns you about this on the environment page.

Windows (Lite) test data types

Random

Generates an alphanumeric string of the length you specify. ~|25| produces 25 characters, and the length can be 1 to 256.

Use it where the value must be unique per run but its content does not matter, such as a new username during a signup test.

A dynamic suite has no fixed membership. It re-evaluates its filter, so a new test case that matches is included without anyone editing the suite.

A prerequisite has two execution modes, and the difference only shows on a data-driven case.

| Enable Visual Testing for the Step | Compares the interface against the baseline at this step |
| Enable Accessibility Testing for the step | Validates this step against accessibility standards |

title: Step options and settings
text:
Step options and settings

Global step timeout

A test plan can set one timeout for every step, and a toggle decides whether it wins against per-step values. The toggle lives under Additional Settings on the run form.

| Test step timeout | Global step timeout | Toggle | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30s (default) | 30s (default) | Off | Global applies, because it matches the default |
| 30s (default) | 60s | Off | Global applies, overriding the default |
| Some steps customised | Updated value | Off | Customised steps keep their own value; the rest take the global |
| Some steps customised | Any value | On | Global applies to every step, overriding customised values |

The pattern is worth stating plainly: with the toggle off the global is a default, and with it on the global is a rule.

Update several steps at once

Select the checkboxes beside the steps you want to change, then click Update Settings in the menu bar.

Bulk update cannot set Pre-Requisite or Retries on step failure. Those two have to be set on each step individually, and a bulk update leaves them untouched rather than warning you.

title: Windows (Lite) step types
text:
Windows (Lite) step types

Standard step types

These seven cover the body of most test cases.

| Step type | Command | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Natural Language | / | A single action or assertion written in Testsigma's readable syntax |
| Step Group | /stepgroup | A reusable sequence of steps, maintained in one place |
| Create a Block | /blocks | A labelled group of steps inside one test case, for structure rather than reuse |
| For Loop | /forloop | Repeat a set of steps a fixed number of times, or once per data row |
| While Loop | /whileloop | Repeat a set of steps until a condition stops being true |
| Custom Function | /function | Call your own code when no natural-language action fits |
| Rest API | /api | Send a REST request as a step, then assert on or store the response |

title: Windows (Lite) step types
text:
Windows (Lite) step types

Conditional step types

Each of these wraps a standard type in a condition, so the wrapped step runs only when the condition holds.

| Step type | Command | What it wraps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| If Natural Language | /if | A natural-language step |
| If Step Group | /if stepgroup | A step group |
| If Custom Function | /if function | A custom function |
| If Rest API | /if api | A REST API step |

Natural-language steps in a Windows (Lite) test case act on the elements captured from the application — see Elements. REST API steps still work here: setting state through an API and verifying it in the application is often faster than driving both through the UI.

Suite has six routes to create a test case, freely mixable in one test:
Type NLP steps in the test case editor (Create Tests → Test Cases); pressing the / key opens the step type menu.

Agentic Learning (Beta) — an agent runs a manual test on the live app and generates the automated test case.
REST API — the POST /test_cases endpoint creates test cases programmatically.

title: Testsigma Support Knowledge — Common Questions
text:
Testsigma Support Knowledge — Common Questions

Why can't I delete a feature or scenario in Testsigma Suite?

product: suite keywords: delete feature, delete scenario, cannot delete, not permitted to delete, trash, permanently delete

In Testsigma Suite, a feature cannot be deleted while it still contains scenarios and test cases that are present in the Trash. Deleting a test case moves it to the Trash rather than removing it, so the parent scenario and feature stay blocked until the Trash is cleared.

Delete in this order:
Delete the test cases associated with the feature and scenario.
Permanently remove those deleted test cases from the Trash. Navigate to Test Cases → Saved Filters → Trash.
Delete the scenario.
Delete the feature.

Why is Atto or Copilot not available in my account?

product: suite keywords: Atto not available, Copilot, unable to generate steps, don't have access, enable Atto, generate test cases

Atto must be enabled for your account before it can be used. If Atto or Copilot options are missing, or generating steps fails because your account has no access to the Atto tool, contact your Customer Success Manager (CSM) and request that Atto be enabled for the account.

Once the feature is enabled, you can generate test cases and use Copilot to perform the required operations.

title: Testsigma Support Knowledge — Common Questions
text:
Testsigma Support Knowledge — Common Questions

Can Testsigma identify an Android element when the package name differs but the resource ID is the same?

product: suite keywords: resource id, package name, android element, apk variants, element identification, app variants

As of June 2026, this capability is not available in the product. A recorded Android element captures the resource ID together with the package name, so the same test case does not carry across app variants that use different package names, such as separate production, release, and UAT builds.

An enhancement request to identify elements by resource ID alone, independent of the package name, has been reviewed and accepted for consideration by the product team. No implementation timeline is committed.

The most common cause is that the element's locator (XPath) no longer matches the application's current DOM — typically because the element was updated in the application after the locator was captured, or the stored XPath was edited. Open the failing step's element and copy its XPath.
Manually validate the XPath in the application (e.g., in browser DevTools) and confirm it correctly identifies/highlights the element in the current DOM.
If it does not, update the element with a locator that matches the current DOM, preferably a simple, stable XPath that avoids deep DOM hierarchy.
Run a dry run of the test case individually to confirm the step passes before executing it in a test plan.

A previous step already switched into the required iframe, and the element is inside that same iframe: remove the nested iframe reference from the element configuration, click Update, and re-execute. Testsigma rewrites an XPath only when Auto Heal fires — i.e., the given locator matched no elements. To iterate table rows with a loop counter, the runtime variable must be wrapped in the pipeline operator: use (//tbody//tr)[$|i|]/td[last()]//button, not (//tbody//tr)[$i]/td[last()]//button. Without $|i| the XPath returns no match and Auto Heal replaces it with a locator pointing to the originally recorded (first-row) element. To stop modification entirely, edit the element and uncheck the Auto Heal option. If clicks pass but each row's menu never opens, a previously opened dropdown overlay may be intercepting clicks: press the ESC key after each row's validation to close the open dropdown, then click the next row.

Why does Testsigma keep creating duplicate elements for the same button, and how do I avoid element sprawl?

product: suite keywords: duplicate element, dynamic DOM, element capture, new page state, Step Groups, reusable components, element sprawl

When the DOM changes dynamically between element captures (for example, similar buttons with shifting attributes), Testsigma treats the updated page state as a new page, so a new element is created on each capture. This is a known behavior in the platform, not a defect in your project. To avoid the resulting duplicates, use Step Groups as reusable components instead of relying on individually captured elements for each occurrence. Building common interactions into Step Groups significantly reduces element sprawl and minimizes maintenance overhead as your test suite scales.

Testsigma does not currently provide a direct option to block specific network or API calls during test recording or execution. If your application only reaches the desired page when a particular API call is blocked (something you can do manually via the browser's inspect/dev tools), the same cannot yet be configured natively in a recorded test.

As a workaround, this can be achieved using external tools such as proxies: route the test traffic through a proxy and configure the proxy to block the required API URL. The test then runs against the application with that call blocked, without any change to the test steps themselves.

There is no separate debug mode toggle; breakpoints are set through Copilot. To pause execution at a specific step:
Open the test case and click the Copilot option within it.
A dropdown appears for setting the initial debug point.
From the dropdown, select the step where execution should pause.
Execution begins from step 1 and pauses at the chosen step, letting you inspect state and debug from there.

Because these rely on element position, they can break in dynamic UIs: if elements are added or the layout changes, index values shift and the locator points to the wrong element or fails.

How do I remove unwanted text from a runtime variable and keep only the value I need?

product: suite keywords: runtime variable, extract data, regex, omit text, add-on, store variable

To strip unwanted text from a runtime variable, install the Extract Data from Runtime Variable Using Regex add-on from the add-ons marketplace and use its NLP step in your test case. Provide a regular expression that captures only the portion you want; the matched value is stored back into a runtime variable. For example, to extract the value between the labels "Policy Holder" and "Premium" in a string like "Policy Holder Regress Ucc Premium", use a lookbehind/lookahead pattern: (?<=Policy Holder\s).+?(?=\sPremium). This keeps only the text between the two labels and discards the surrounding words.

This happens when the actual content in the two runs differs. A variable populated by a mailbox (email) function contains the full email body, while a hardcoded variable usually holds only a trimmed portion — so a regex tuned to the shorter text may not match the longer content. Fix it by anchoring the regex to a stable label immediately before the value and matching only the value's characters, instead of bounding it with surrounding sentence text. For example, to extract a policy number that follows the label "Policy Number", use (?<=Policy Number\s)[A-Za-z0-9]+. This pattern works whether the source text is hardcoded or retrieved through mailbox functions, because it depends only on the label directly preceding the value.

If the Generate TOTP add-on step generates a code, stores it in the runtime variable, and enters it correctly, but the application still rejects it, the cause is almost always the secret key rather than the add-on. The secret key configured in the test is no longer recognized by the identity provider — for example, Microsoft Entra ID policies can automatically remove or invalidate TOTP registrations, which also shows up as the registration disappearing from the account's Security info page shortly after it is added. To resolve:
Check with your IT team whether any policy removes or invalidates TOTP registrations for the account.
Once the registration is stable, re-enroll the authenticator method and obtain the new secret key.
Update the secret key in the Testsigma test step and re-run.

The "verify that the current page displays text" validation historically checked the application's XML/page source: if the text existed anywhere in the page source, the condition passed — even when the matching element was hidden (for example, inside a collapsed dropdown or an off-screen menu). So an If condition could evaluate to true for text a user cannot see, sending execution down the wrong branch and failing on a later click against a non-interactable element. The underlying NLP logic has since been updated so that text present in the DOM but not displayed on the UI no longer causes the condition to evaluate to true; existing test cases need no modification. If an If block still misbehaves, inspect the element's recorded code in the test results to see the page source captured at runtime and check for duplicate hidden occurrences of the text.
